Eventually the leg kick was added back, but smaller and more controlled. Crow-Armstrong’s stride timing remained inconsistent but adjustable.
“What he lacks in timing he can make up in bat speed,” Mallee said. “What the leg kick did was allow him to start very early and move towards the pitcher in a slow and controlled linear move. … It is no longer a violent crash forward but a smooth flow. Then when his eyes tell him it’s time to swing, his foot goes into the ground. His adjustability is incredible and now he can be on a 100 mph fastball and downshift to offspeed. This is when he took off.”
Those tweaks, combined with a move to the leadoff spot, put Crow-Armstrong on a tear and led to his second All-Star selection. In his last 102 games, dating to May 26, he’s posted a .307/.398/.679 line with 25 doubles, 39 home runs, 84 RBIs and a 1.077 OPS.
“I think this year showed me how long the season really is,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Last year, the struggle was a couple weeks at the beginning of the year. This was over a month. And now it feels we’ve been on this good run for a long, long time. So I think I’ve just understood how long the season actually is.”
His 2025 second-half decline highlighted what he needed to do to become more consistent in his mechanical work and game planning. Mallee recalls when first working with Crow-Armstrong at Triple A he had a “see-ball, hit-ball” approach and didn’t really use the scouting reports. Now Crow-Armstrong studiously looks at how lefties pitch to left-handed hitters and the way he’s been attacked in the past. He regularly talks about approaches with his teammates and goes up to the plate with a plan. Experience matters, too. Getting to see pitchers more frequently over the course of his career gives Crow-Armstrong a better understanding of what to look for.
“When we first started, he couldn’t even evaluate his misses,” Mallee said. “Now he’s got the pitchers in the buckets. He knows how to read the scouting reports. He knows how to anticipate, and he’s very good instinctively. Sometimes he can feel and sense. And I said, honor your gut, man. You have these instincts, buddy. They’re given to you. If you feel like something’s going to happen, then honor it and stay with it and then trust it. And if it doesn’t come out that way, it’s OK because you had a plan.”
Although he will likely always be on the higher side of swing rates, Crow-Armstrong made a change in May to not go out of the zone just because he’s capable of getting to those pitches. By July 27, he had tallied more walks this season than the previous three big-league years combined.
“I am a lot more repeatable this year, I can go into the cage and I can know that I’m going to do the same three things before I swing,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Whereas last year, there was something new every day. Other than that, though, yeah, it’s all mental.”
The power production started to emerge in abundance last year, surprising some around the league that the speedy, elite defender put up 31 home runs. That didn’t surprise Cubs assistant general manager Jared Banner. He got his first in-person look at Crow-Armstrong shortly after the New York Mets drafted him at No. 19 in 2020. Banner, the Mets’ executive director of player development at that time, had only seen some video of Crow-Armstrong play because the COVID-19 pandemic cut short his high school senior season. During a camp scrimmage at the Mets’ complex in Port St. Lucie, Fla., Crow-Armstrong slugged a home run with a 107 mph exit velocity.
It immediately grabbed Banner’s attention.
“That’s just not something you see very often from a high school kid who’s not a huge monster, just freakish power for someone of that size,” Banner said to the Tribune. “It gave me a sense that he had a ton of capacity to impact the baseball. He was already strong and had bat speed, but as he continues to grow up and mature then he’s going to hit the ball even harder. And once you’re up in that territory, it’s a leap.”
A torn labrum in his right shoulder six games into his pro career ended his 2021 season with surgery and, by keeping him under the radar with the lack of game action, helped the Cubs acquire Crow-Armstrong at the trade deadline that year.
“I think Pete always knew he was a superstar, it was the rest of us that had to catch up,” Banner said. “Superstars know how to handle the attention. They know how to handle the pressure. Heavy is the head that wears a crown, and he wears it really well.”
Crow-Armstrong has already broken multiple franchise records. One more remains in play for the final six games of the regular season. With two more stolen bases, he will become just the seventh player in MLB history to record a 40-home-run, 40-steal season.
“Stats-wise, where I’m at now, I frame it as if I keep playing well, then we’re probably gonna be in pretty good shape. But I can appreciate the persistence I’ve had and kind of the calm that I found. I guess I always know that I’m going to turn it on at some point, but I’m proud of how I did this year. I think it was a very honest showing all year of everything.”
Crow-Armstrong’s frustrations from that late August series in Arizona didn’t last long.
Back at Wrigley Field after an off day, he collected two singles against the Cincinnati Reds and then went off: a three-home-run game Aug. 29 and two more home runs the following game. Crow-Armstrong experienced a newfound satisfaction that even though he endured a tough West Coast trip not long after a 3-for-28 stretch earlier in August, he kept things in perspective.
Two tough weeks don’t have to define a season.
“One thing that I’ve talked about with people is the best players really minimize how long their poor periods are,” Crow-Armstrong said. “And I’ve started to kind of notice that where if I’m feeling really s−−−−− for a couple days, I’m making sure, and I don’t know how I do it, but I’m making sure that it’s only a couple days, and I salvaged that third day, or that fourth day, or that fifth day. I let s−−− snowball last year, and that’s not going to happen to me. I’m not willing to do that.”
His incredible performance this year has reached the point of shifting the question from whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP to whether he will be unanimously chosen by the 30 Baseball Writers’ Association of America voters, something that has happened only 10 times in the National League since this iteration of the award started in 1931. The individual honor awaiting him in November is something he’s still grappling with and trying not to think about, let alone wanting to discuss, even with the regular season nearly complete.
“Someone’s gonna have to teach me what an individual season really means if stuff doesn’t really roll our way (in the playoffs),” Crow-Armstrong said. “I think that’s probably the hardest part about a win or a loss is, regardless, I’m going to focus on one of the two and probably take away from the individual stuff. But as long as I gave people something to look forward to going to the park, then that’s a big enough win for me, I think, with all the individual season stuff.”
Nearly four years before Crow-Armstrong was born, Sammy Sosa played a big role in creating the next generation of Cubs fans during his electric 66-home-run 1998 season that culminated in the NL MVP award. For him to do something at that level this year, for such a historic franchise, must feel surreal, right?
“I don’t want to believe it just yet,” Crow-Armstrong said. “So when we get there, you can ask me.”

title: Marcelo Mayer and His Dad's Red Sox Exit Comments Raise Eyebrows
author: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
body:
For the second straight year, the Boston Red Sox traded an infielder who was expected to be a part of the club's long-term plans to the San Francisco Giants in a surprise move.
Last year, it was Rafael Devers. This year, it was former top prospect Marcelo Mayer. When it comes to both players, it's unfortunate how things worked out. Both clearly have immense talent, but other factors came into the picture and Boston opted to move on. This summer, the Red Sox traded Mayer to the Giants in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. It was a surprising deal, but Miller has been good in the majors for Boston since.
Mayer, who has been dealing with injuries, made his Giants debut on Monday and went 0-for-4. On top of that, Susan Slusser of the San Francisco Chronicle shared a fascinating column about Mayer, featuring comments from both the young infielder, and his father, about his Boston exit.
The Red Sox Moved On
"Obviously, it didn’t go the way I wanted,” Mayer said of his Red Sox tenure, “And obviously, outside the lines, it’s a lot over there.”
On top of this, Slusser reported that Mayer and his family let the Red Sox's front office know that they would be "comfortable" with a trade before the deadline.
Mayer's father dug in a bit more, to say the least.
"When I found out, I jumped 30 feet in the air,” Enrique Mayer said to Slusser. “I can’t explain how happy we are. ... “In Boston, if you’re going well, you’re a god and if you’re struggling, they’re going to tear you apart. He didn’t come out as hot this year and the fans thought he didn’t care — that’s the most ridiculous thing to say about a major-league baseball player, people don’t know the sacrifices and work it takes just to get there. But he got a bad rap and if you get a little bit of one in Boston, it just snowballs.”
This is a fascinating insight into one of the most surprising deals of the summer from the people directly involved. Now, of course, Mayer is just 23 years old and is a player for another team. It would be more surprising if he dug in more than he did with his comments. But he's not wrong. He's someone who struggled offensively, or with injuries, and took a lot of heat from Boston fans as a result. Around the time of the trade, the heat got to the point that Red Sox chief baseball officer Craig Breslow joined "The Greg Hill Show" on WEEI and denied "nonsense" rumors about alleged off-field issues between Mayer and Roman Anthony.
Mayer's father's comments unsurprisingly were more pointed. At the end of the day, unfortunately things didn't work out between the two sides in the majors. The talent is there and if Mayer can stay healthy, he's going to be very good in San Francisco. In Boston, he wasn't able to and then the fanbase got very loud. For Boston, there are now long-term questions at shortstop. Could Franklin Arias be the guy now? Maybe, but he's also young and it's clearly too early to assume after what happened with Mayer.

title: Pete Crow-Armstrong is chasing more than just an MVP
author: Kendall Baker
body:
Yahoo Sports AM is our daily newsletter that keeps you up to date on all things sports. Sign up here to get it every weekday morning.
⚾️ Forget MVP. PCA is chasing history
Pete Crow-Armstrong wrapped up the NL MVP award weeks ago. Now, in the final week of the regular season, the Cubs centerfielder is looking to put the finishing touches on one of the greatest all-around campaigns in baseball history.
Triple threat: PCA might not pitch like his onetime MVP competition Shohei Ohtani, but he does wield the best glove in the league in addition to his otherworldly combination of power and speed.
- At the plate he's batting .280 with an NL-best .949 OPS on the strength of 45 home runs. Yes, the speedy centerfielder is now tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. He also leads the majors in runs (118) and extra-base hits (83), and ranks third in RBI (107).
- In the field he leads all players in outs above average (26) and fielding run value (27). His 50% success rate (8 of 16) on 5-star catches (those with a Statcast probability of 0-25%) is also by far the best in the majors.
Put another way: He's having the best offensive season of anyone outside of Yordan Alvarez, but while the Astros slugger spends almost all of his time at designated hitter, PCA has also been the single best fielder in baseball at any position.
Big picture: Add it all up, and Crow-Armstrong has amassed 10.4 wins above replacement at FanGraphs, making him just the seventh position player this century to post a 10-fWAR season. But as impressive as that is in a vacuum, it's in the comparison to his peers where it transcends to historic territory.
- Perhaps you've heard of the other three men to accomplish that feat: Babe Ruth (3x), Rogers Hornsby (2x) and Mickey Mantle. Adjusted for era, PCA's season has to be considered one of the greatest ever. And to think, we almost didn't get it.
Midseason change: It's easy to forget now, but PCA had a terrible spring, batting .224 with 6 HR and a .676 OPS in 55 games from Opening Day through May 26. As the poor results kept coming and he drifted further away from the player who'd shown flashes of superstardom a year earlier, he and Chicago's coaching staff decided to drastically alter his stance.
- The changes, as laid out by WSJ's Jared Diamond ($), were three-fold: He stands closer to the plate and deeper in the box, his legs are a foot closer together, and he holds his hands at his chest with the bat pointing up rather than at shoulder-level with the bat parallel to the ground.
- Safe to say it worked. In 101 games since the changes began taking hold, he's hitting .307 with 39 home runs and a 1.079 OPS.
The last word: "You're grateful to see things like this," Cubs manager Craig Counsell said last week after PCA's seventh multi-homer game of the season. "And you're grateful that the fans get to see a season like this, because they're going to talk about it. They're going to tell their kids about it. They're going to tell their grandkids about seasons like this."
🌍 The world in photos
🇺🇸 Los Angeles, California
The Rams destroyed the Giants in their home opener, 28-6, behind huge games from Matthew Stafford (22/31, 327 yards, 4 TD) and Davante Adams (8 catches, 195 yards, 2 TD). New York, meanwhile, joined the injured QB club* as Jaxson Dart was knocked out in the first quarter with what appears to be a sprained MCL.
Climbing the leaderboard: With 427 career passing touchdowns, Stafford passed Philip Rivers (425) for sixth-most in NFL history. He'll need to play at least another couple seasons to catch Brett Favre (508) in fifth, and may have a little more trouble catching Aaron Rodgers (528), Peyton Manning (539), Drew Brees (571) and Tom Brady (649).
🇫🇷 Clairefontaine-en-Yvelines, France
Zinedine Zidane oversaw his first training session on Monday since becoming France's new head coach, with his first test coming in Friday's Nations League match against Turkey. The international break, which at 16 days is the longest ever, runs through Oct. 6.
Why so long? This is the first such break under FIFA's new calendar, which has been reconfigured to limit travel and minimize disruptions to domestic club schedules. Instead of three short breaks in the fall and one in the spring, there are now two in the fall and one in the spring.
🇨🇦 Montreal, Canada
Belgium's Remco Evenepoel dominated the field on Sunday for his record-tying fourth time trial world title, becoming the first cyclist to win the event four years in a row. That continues an excellent year that also saw the two-time Olympic champion finish second to Tadej Pogačar in the Tour de France.
The secret to his success: At 5-foot-7, Evenepoel is smaller than most elite time trialists, but what he lacks in mass he makes up for with his uniquely compact riding position. "He can almost put his head into his trunk and into his arms, and he's still able to look forward," says Evenepoel's physio. "That's why they call him 'the bullet.'"
*QB injury updates: Chicago's Caleb Williams (hamstring) "will likely miss some time" but avoided a serious injury and Washington's Jayden Daniels (dislocated elbow) will meet with specialists this week. On the flip side, Minnesota's Kyler Murray (concussion) and Atlanta's Michael Penix Jr. (ACL surgery recovery) will both start in Week 3.
👟 Mbappé moves On
In June, Kylian Mbappé featured centrally in Nike's "Rip the Script" World Cup short film, shortly before tearing through defenses in Nike boots throughout the tournament. Just three months later, his long-time relationship with the Swoosh has ended. Mbappé is moving On… or to On, in this case.
Catch up: Swiss sportswear brand On announced on Friday that it's entering football alongside the French superstar. Mbappé will be a global ambassador for the brand, working closely with product teams in developing football footwear and apparel.
What it means: This is perhaps the most ambitious extension of On's brand yet, as it tries to establish itself at the highest ranks of the world's most popular sport. However, the company has a track record in precisely this sort of endeavor, executed with a very similar playbook.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes: The last time On shocked the sports world with a signing of this magnitude, the brand was a lesser-known commodity. Its prize in 2019? Swiss tennis legend Roger Federer, who invested in the company and supported its efforts to build a tennis business. On's efforts in tennis, anchored by Federer and aided by stars like Iga Świątek and Ben Shelton, demonstrate its ability to grow from a nonexistent presence to a major player at a sport's elite levels. With Mbappé in tow, it will try to make the same leap in football.
This is an excerpt from Monday's edition of Yahoo Sports Biz, our new sports business newsletter. Sign up here to get on the list.
🏀 NBA preseason power rankings
With the NBA season tipping off in less than a month (Oct. 20), Yahoo Sports' Kevin O'Connor has ranked every team's chances of winning the 2027 NBA Championship, while also surveying what's changed during the offseason, what's exciting and what's concerning for each team.
⚽️ Barcelona are unstoppable
Barcelona have opened their 2026-27 campaign in another stratosphere, laying waste to the competition with a goal-scoring frenzy the likes of which haven't been seen in nearly a century.
36 goals for, 8 against: Barça are undefeated in eight matches entering the international break, scoring 31 goals across their first seven La Liga fixtures (second-most in league history behind Sevilla in 1940), and 36 if you include their Champions League opener (their most through eight matches since 1935).
- Barcelona 5, Elche 0
- Barcelona 2, Athletic Club 0
- Barcelona 5, Rayo Vallecano 2
- Barcelona 5, Valenica 0
- Barcelona 5, Feyenoord Rotterdam 1
- Barcelona 4, Levante 2
- Barcelona 7, Racing Santander 2
- Barcelona 3, Sevilla 1
Dynamic duo: At the center of the carnage are Brazilian striker Raphinha and Spanish winger Lamine Yamal, who've combined for 22 goals and nine assists on the young season. Raphinha's 12 domestic goals lead La Liga by a wide margin, while his three assists are tied for second; Lamine's seven goals are tied for second, and his four assists are tied for first.
Go deeper: This is the best Barcelona have looked under Hansi Flick (The Athletic)
📺 Watchlist: Tuesday, Sept. 22
⚾️ Rays at Yankees
The AL East rivals begin their four-game series with a split doubleheader (1:05pm ET, ESPN+; 7:05pm, TBS), and though the division hasn't been decided yet, the race is all but over. The Rays (95-60) have a six-game lead over the Yankees (89-66), who therefore must sweep this series to have any shot of avoiding the wild card.
Best of the rest: The wild-card bound Red Sox (84-72) host the Guardians (81-75), who hold a one-game lead in the AL Central (6:45pm); the White Sox (80-76), currently in the third wild card and chasing Cleveland for the division, visit the Royals (7:40pm); the Rangers (78-78) host the Mets (8:05pm) with a one-game lead in the AL West over the Astros (77-79), who visit the Mariners in the nightcap (9:40pm).
⚾️ WPBL Championship, Game 5
The Women's Professional Baseball League will crown its inaugural champion tonight (7pm, ESPN+) when the San Francisco Firebells — who've fought back from an 0-2 deficit — take on the Los Angeles Queens in a decisive Game 5.
Players to watch: This series features arguably the two biggest names in women's baseball. The Firebells are led by No. 1 pick Kelsie Whitmore, a two-way player who hit a league-leading 11 HR this season while also starting six games on the mound; the Queens boast Mo'ne Davis, the trailblazing star of the 2014 Little League World Series.
More to watch:
- 🏀 WNBA: Lynx at Fever (8pm, ESPN); Sparks at Aces (10pm, ESPN) … Minnesota (32-10) clinches the No. 1 seed with a win.
- 🏒 NHL Preaseason: Panthers at Hurricanes (7pm, NHL); Golden Knights at Sharks (10pm, NHL) … T-minus one week until the regular season begins.
🌍 GeoSports
GeoSports is back in Yahoo Sports AM, and I'll be writing the questions every Tuesday.
How to play: You'll be asked five trivia questions that combine sports with geography. Tap where it happened! The closer you are, the more points you get.

Triple threat: PCA might not pitch like his onetime MVP competition Shohei Ohtani, but he does wield the best glove in the league in addition to his otherworldly combination of power and speed.
- At the plate he's batting .280 with an NL-best .949 OPS on the strength of 45 home runs. Yes, the speedy centerfielder is now tied with Kyle Schwarber for the MLB lead. He also leads the majors in runs (118) and extra-base hits (83), and ranks third in RBI (107).
- In the field he leads all players in outs above average (26) and fielding run value (27). His 50% success rate (8 of 16) on 5-star catches (those with a Statcast probability of 0-25%) is also by far the best in the majors.
Put another way: He's having the best offensive season of anyone outside of Yordan Alvarez, but while the Astros slugger spends almost all of his time at designated hitter, PCA has also been the single best fielder in baseball at any position.

But as impressive as that is in a vacuum, it's in the comparison to his peers where it transcends to historic territory.
- Perhaps you've heard of the other three men to accomplish that feat: Babe Ruth (3x), Rogers Hornsby (2x) and Mickey Mantle. Adjusted for era, PCA's season has to be considered one of the greatest ever. And to think, we almost didn't get it.

title: Oneil Cruz milestone is a reminder Pirates have barely seen his ceiling
author: Emma Lingan
body:
Oneil Cruz lost more than two months of his season to the injured list and still managed to put himself in the same sentence as Barry Bonds and Andrew McCutchen. That should tell the Pittsburgh Pirates everything they need to know about just how much upside remains.
With his solo home run off Michael Wacha on Sunday against the Kansas City Royals, Cruz reached 20 homers for the season and became just the third player in franchise history to record at least 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases in three consecutive years.
Bonds did it. McCutchen did it. Now Cruz has, too. But unlike a milestone that feels like the culmination of a player’s greatness, this one feels more like another glimpse at what Pittsburgh still hasn’t fully gotten to see.
Oneil Cruz gave Pirates another glimpse of what a healthy season could bring with third straight 20-20 season
Cruz missed more than two months on the injured list this season, yet still managed to reach 20 home runs and 20 steals. That makes the accomplishment less a reflection of his ceiling than a reminder of how high that ceiling might actually be.
That has always been the fascination with Cruz. At 6-foot-7 with some of the loudest raw tools in baseball, there has never been much mystery about what he is capable of physically. Few players can hit a baseball as hard, throw it as hard or move as well at his size. The question has always been whether those tools could consistently translate into star-level production over the course of a full season.
Unfortunately, that full season remains elusive. Injuries have interrupted Cruz repeatedly, including again in 2026. Yet even without the benefit of a complete year, he continues to pile up accomplishments that put him in franchise company with players who defined entire eras of Pirates baseball. That should leave Pittsburgh wondering what a healthy Cruz season could actually look like.
Thirty home runs? Thirty stolen bases? More? None of those possibilities feel especially far-fetched considering he reached 20-20 this year despite losing such a significant chunk of the schedule.
There are still parts of Cruz’s game that can improve. His swing-and-miss tendencies can become frustrating, and his offensive production has occasionally come in streaks. But the Pirates don't need to imagine what happens if Cruz suddenly becomes a completely different player. They simply need to see what happens if the version they already have stays on the field long enough.
For a Pirates team that is going to miss the postseason despite taking a legitimate step forward offensively, Cruz remains one of the biggest reasons to believe there is another level available in 2027. Three straight 20-20 seasons already place him next to Bonds and McCutchen, but it still feels like Cruz is only beginning to show what he can become..

title: Vinnie Pasquantino, Daniel Lynch IV Turn in Strong Weeks: Royals Stock Up, Stock Down
author: Brian Sparks; Unknown
body:
Welcome to “Stock Up, Stock Down,” where every week, the Royals On SI staff writers highlight Kansas City Royals players who have stood out or had a rough week. From the lineup to the pitching staff, we’ll dive into who is trending up and who is trending down.
Kansas City did not have its best week, going 1-5 over the last seven days. The Royals’ lone win came during their series loss to the Houston Astros. Let’s take a look at some players who stood out and some who sat down.
Stock Up: Players Who Stood Out Over the Past Week
Daniel Lynch IV
In the Royals’ lone win over the past week, Daniel Lynch IV had his best start of the season since joining the rotation. Lynch tossed five strong innings, allowing just two hits, no earned runs and striking out three.
Lynch was having a fantastic year out of the bullpen, serving as a bright spot for a group that has struggled all season. Kansas City decided to test Lynch in the rotation, but unfortunately, his production has not been the same as it was in the bullpen. This week, however, he was able to get things rolling.
Vinnie Pasquantino
Vinnie Pasquantino has swung the bat very well over the last week, putting on a power display. Over the last seven days, he is slashing .375/.412/.938, with three of his hits being home runs.
This is an encouraging sign from the first baseman, who has had a limited season due to injuries and a slow start to the year. Pasquantino is looking to finish the season on a strong note.
Nick Loftin
Utility man Nick Loftin has had a hot stretch at the plate over the past week. He has posted a .438 average in his last 16 at-bats. His plate approach has looked great, as he has struck out just once and recorded a double as well.
Stock Down: Players Who Struggled Over the Past Week
Nate Pearson
Relief arm Nate Pearson did not have his best stuff over the past seven days. In just 2 2/3 innings, he allowed six earned runs on seven hits, including one home run. He struck out three as the right-hander looks to bounce back and finish the year strong.
Maikel Garcia
Maikel Garcia has not been at his best since returning from the injured list. In his first 16 at-bats back in the lineup, the third baseman has recorded just one hit. He has collected two RBIs but appears to be dealing with a slow start since returning from the injury.
Kyle Isbel
Much like Garcia, Kyle Isbel has not been seeing the ball well at the plate. He has collected just one hit in his last 13 at-bats and has struck out four times. The hope is the center fielder can finish the year strong following this slump.

Kansas City did not have its best week, going 1-5 over the last seven days. The Royals’ lone win came during their series loss to the Houston Astros. Let’s take a look at some players who stood out and some who sat down.
Stock Up: Players Who Stood Out Over the Past Week
Daniel Lynch IV
In the Royals’ lone win over the past week, Daniel Lynch IV had his best start of the season since joining the rotation. Lynch tossed five strong innings, allowing just two hits, no earned runs and striking out three.
Lynch was having a fantastic year out of the bullpen, serving as a bright spot for a group that has struggled all season. Kansas City decided to test Lynch in the rotation, but unfortunately, his production has not been the same as it was in the bullpen. This week, however, he was able to get things rolling.
Vinnie Pasquantino
Vinnie Pasquantino has swung the bat very well over the last week, putting on a power display. Over the last seven days, he is slashing .375/.412/.938, with three of his hits being home runs.
This is an encouraging sign from the first baseman, who has had a limited season due to injuries and a slow start to the year. Pasquantino is looking to finish the season on a strong note.
Nick Loftin
Utility man Nick Loftin has had a hot stretch at the plate over the past week. He has posted a .438 average in his last 16 at-bats. His plate approach has looked great, as he has struck out just once and recorded a double as well.
Stock Down: Players Who Struggled Over the Past Week
Nate Pearson
Relief arm Nate Pearson did not have his best stuff over the past seven days. In just 2 2/3 innings, he allowed six earned runs on seven hits, including one home run. He struck out three as the right-hander looks to bounce back and finish the year strong.
Maikel Garcia
Maikel Garcia has not been at his best since returning from the injured list. In his first 16 at-bats back in the lineup, the third baseman has recorded just one hit. He has collected two RBIs but appears to be dealing with a slow start since returning from the injury.
Kyle Isbel
Much like Garcia, Kyle Isbel has not been seeing the ball well at the plate. He has collected just one hit in his last 13 at-bats and has struck out four times. The hope is the center fielder can finish the year strong following this slump.

title: Orioles news: Pete Alonso stays hot
author: Stacey
body:
Happy Tuesday, Camden Chatters!
Last night, we got a reprieve from the misery that has been Orioles baseball lately. And we got it mostly thanks to Pete Alonso (who else). Alonso hit his 39th and 40th home runs of the season last night, powering the Orioles to a 4-3 victory over the Blue Jays. He's now the 10th Oriole to have a 40-homer season, and his 108 RBI are the most in the American League. It's Alonso's first 40-homer season since 2023 and his fourth in his career.
Oh, and Alonso just happened to hit two homers on the day that his son, Teddy, celebrated his first birthday. What a guy.
Gunnar Henderson also homered, his 24th. Henderson had three hits in the game. Starting pitcher Shane Baz struggled through a three-run first inning, but went on to pitch 6.2 innings without allowing a run after the first. You can get the full details of the win in Alex Church's recap.
By my estimation, the Orioles have been out of the race since the Red Sox swept them in early September. Now it seems like the White Sox or Guardians will take the final Wild Card spot, with the other winning the AL Central. The Blue Jays are basically out of it as well, and the Orioles have the chance in this series to ensure their AL East foe is truly finished.
The Orioles won't go to the playoffs and they won't have a winning season, but they can put the nail in the coffin for the Blue Jays. And if the Orioles win tonight and tomorrow, these teams will leave Baltimore with the Blue Jays in last place instead of the Orioles. It's not something to get excited about, but it's always preferable to NOT be in last place.
Tonight, it'll be an old-man special as Chris Bassitt (37) and Max Scherzer (42) face off. It's a rematch of the game on 9/11, in which both pitchers went five innings. Scherzer allowed six runs and took the loss, while Bassitt allowed two runs and got the win. I wouldn't hate to see a repeat of that. The weather forecast today is pretty dicey, so hopefully they get the game in. I mean, I guess. Would it really matter if they didn't?
Links
How one swing exposed a season's worth of frustration for the Orioles – The Baltimore Banner
This was written about what happened after the Orioles lost on Sunday, but the contents have been a hot topic in Birdland. Specifically, how Craig Albernaz reacted to the press after Jeremiah Jackson grounded out on the first pitch against a struggling pitcher.
Alonso homers twice to reach 40 and give Orioles 4-3 win over Blue Jays – MASN Sports
Roch Kubatko's game story has plenty of quotes about how amazing Pete Alonso is, but also includes some info on Samuel Basallo, who exited last night's game after being hit square in the mask with a foul ball. Be ok, Samuel! Knocks to the head are scary.
Wehiwa Aloy and Joseph Dzierwa Named Orioles Minor League Player and Pitcher of the Year – MLB.com
The two awardees were at Camden Yards last night to accept, and both hopped into the broadcast booth to talk about their seasons. If you've never heard those two names spoken aloud before, here is your lesson. Wahiwa is pronounced Vuh-Hee-Vah. Dzierwa is pronounced Jer-Wah. Got it?
Birthdays and History
Is today your birthday? Happy birthday! You have a ton of Orioles birthday buddies, each more forgettable than the last. But because today is their birthday, today we remember them:
- Chris Ellis (34), eight games in 2021-22
- Luis García (51), six games in 2002
- César Devarez (57), 16 games in 1995-96.
- P.J. Forbes (59), nine games in 1998
- John Stefero (67), 61 games in 1983 and 1986
- Bob Harrison (b. 1930, d. 2023), two games in 1955-56
On this day in 1961, Jim Gentile hit his fifth grand slam of the year. That tied him with Ernie Banks for the most in a season. The current record is six, held by Travis Hafner and Don Mattingly.
In 1966, the Orioles clinched their first AL pennant with 6-1 victory over the Kansas City Athletics. Jim Palmer, just 20 years old, pitched a complete game.
In 1973, the Orioles defeated the Milwaukee Brewers 7-1 to clinch the division. Al Bumbry hit three triples in the win.
In 2012, the Orioles beat the Red Sox 9-6 in 13 innings, marking their 87th win of the year. They scored three runs in the top of the 13th with RBI hits from Jim Thome, Endy Chavez, and Manny Machado. Mark Reynolds and Adam Jones homered earlier. They remained one game out of the AL East after the Yankees pulled off an extra-innings win of their own.

title: Baseball’s Best Pitchers Aren’t Worth What They Used to Be (But Its Best Batters Are)
body:
On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. This season will either match last year’s all-time full-season low of three 200-plus-inning pitchers, or further reduce the record, depending on whether Michael Wacha (who’s sitting at 194 1/3 frames) joins Sandy Alcantara and Cristopher Sánchez in the 200-inning club in his final start.
Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. PCA, for example, has played in every Cubs game this season, and started all but one. (As of today, he’s the majors’ sole 700-plate-appearance man.) We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. And if we want to cite WAR, well, that’s easy: With six Cubs games to go, PCA’s season already ranks among the 50 best batting years in big league history, and above every season in the past half century save for four by Bonds, two by Judge, and one by Bobby Witt Jr.
In 2026, pitchers tend not to throw enough pitches or innings to reach famous milestones in single games, single seasons, or careers, so the case for Miz amazement can’t be made by hailing his membership in exclusive, storied clubs. With one regular-season start remaining, the Miz hasn’t quite cracked the top 350 seasons by pitching WAR. (No pitcher has posted a double-digit-WAR season since the Big Unit in 2001.) The 300-strikeout club has been closed to new recruits since Cole and his teammate Justin Verlander went in together in 2019. As for old-school wins, he’s tied for second in the Senior Circuit with 15, not that anyone pays much attention to that column on the player page.
To appreciate the Miz, we must resort to rate stats and modest minimums. Among pitchers with at least 160 innings in a season, Misiorowski ranks 13th in park- and league-adjusted ERA, 12th in park- and league-adjusted FIP, third in WHIP and strikeout-minus-walk rate, and second in strikeout rate. He has the lowest opponent batting average and rate of hits allowed per nine innings, too, which would be more eye-popping if people still cared about batting average or if the league were hitting more than .244. Ultimately, the summation rests on the smallest of samples: a single pitch. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. original_body:
On Sunday, as MLB’s regular season reached its one-week warning, the two most spectacular players of 2026 strutted their stuff. In Cincinnati, Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong singled, doubled, and hit his 45th home run in a 9-1 trouncing of the Reds. (He also stole his 38th base, putting him on the precipice of joining the 40-40 club.) Hours later, at Camden Yards, Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski held the Orioles to one hit and lowered his ERA to 1.86 as the Brewers blanked Baltimore 3-0 for their major-league-leading (and franchise-record) 98th win.
A season’s most sensational player isn’t always its most valuable player—see Cal Raleigh last year—but PCA and the Miz check both boxes. They lead the majors in FanGraphs WAR for hitters and pitchers, respectively, and will win the MVP and Cy Young awards in the National League (which has established itself as the stronger circuit by owning the American League 375–323 in interleague play). PCA and the Miz; the Miz and PCA: Already All-Stars in 2025, they’ve made large leaps this year. The Cub has bolstered his bat speed and drawn more walks; the Brewer has upped his pitch speed and issued fewer walks. Born nine days apart in the spring of 2002, the two 24-year-old terrors of the NL Central have set the standards for hitting and pitching excellence and, in the process, made themselves the player stories of the season. In an MLB campaign whose compressed standings have caused fans to wonder which teams, if any, are actually good (especially in the AL, where the .500 Rangers lead the AL West), the left-handed hitter and right-handed hurler—whose clubs may meet in October—have left little doubt about their own extreme skills.
There’s also little doubt about how those skills stack up against each other—or, at least, what those skills are worth when they’re applied on the field. The “WAR leader” label lumps PCA and Misiorowski together as peerless players. If we had to choose between them, though, the answer would be easy: The Miz wins most of their head-to-head battles, but PCA wins the WAR. Crow-Armstrong, who’s hit .280/.371/.578 with superlative defense in center, has been much more valuable than Misiorowski, who’s held hitters to a .159/.225/.250 line and who’s struck out 247 batters (including PCA six times) while walking only 42 (including PCA twice). That’s no surprise: It’s now the norm for baseball’s best hitter to be a good deal better, WAR-wise, than baseball’s best pitcher. Which, in turn, tells us a lot about how hitter and pitcher usage—and entertainment value—have evolved.
Take Sunday’s action. PCA played the whole game in center, even though the Cubs had built a comfortable lead by the halfway point. The Miz, meanwhile, exited after three innings and 44 pitches, with the Brew Crew clinging to a 1-0 lead. With home field advantage throughout October up for grabs, Milwaukee still had something to play for. But the Brewers elected to take it easy on their flamethrower, who has already exceeded his 2025 workload (including the playoffs) by 28 innings. As a result, Misiorowski amassed just 62 percent of the WAR PCA did on Sunday—and, on the whole, he’s managed only 63 percent of the WAR PCA has produced this season (6.5 vs. 10.4).
It wasn’t always the case that baseball’s best hitter would leave baseball’s best pitcher in his dust on the combined WAR leaderboard. The chart below compares the values of FanGraphs’ hitting and pitching WAR leaders for each season dating back to the beginning of the DH era in 1973. To smooth out year-to-year variation, each bar represents a five-year rolling average of the annual hitter-minus-pitcher WAR gaps from the listed season plus the four preceding seasons. Thus, the value for 1973 is really the average of the figures from 1969 to 1973, and the value for 2026 is really the average of the figures from 2022 to 2026.
At the dawn of the DH era, when the iron men of the mound were still routinely topping 300 innings, the best pitchers were worth more than the best hitters. Pitchers also reigned supreme around the turn of the century, when the likes of Roger Clemens, Kevin Brown, and Randy Johnson were still topping 250 dominant innings, and Pedro Martínez posted the best pitching season ever by fWAR in 1999 (in a then-paltry 213 1/3 innings, which would lead both leagues in 2026). All in all, from the beginning of the DH era through the end of the 20th century, the leading hitter in any given year was worth only about half a WAR more than the leading pitcher, on average. From 1970 through 2000, the best hitter out-WARed the best pitcher 18 times, while a pitcher took the top spot 13 times. The battle for the title of baseball’s best player was typically close to a toss-up between the most overpowering pitcher and the biggest bat.
Over the past quarter century, though, the hitters have won in a walk. Beginning with 2001, when Barry Bonds morphed into his BALCO-boosted final form, the leading hitter has been about two wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher, enough to declare a conclusive victor despite the metric’s margin of error. During that span, best hitters have led best pitchers 25 seasons to one, with only Corbin Burnes’s slim edge over Trea Turner in 2021 preventing a clean sweep. And the gap is growing: Over the past five years, the leading hitter has been a full four wins better, on average, than the leading pitcher. In other words, baseball’s best pitchers aren’t worth what they used to be—but its best batters are.
This isn’t just a function of the no. 1 hitter lapping the no. 1 pitcher; although the average leads are less pronounced, the same trend appears when we expand the pool to each year’s top five hitters and top five pitchers.
The wide disparity in recent seasons stems in part from an unusually strong run by baseball’s best hitters. The average of 10.4 WAR generated by the hitting WAR leaders in the past five years (Aaron Judge three times, and Ronald Acuña Jr. and PCA once each) is the highest total of any five-season stretch since Bonds, Alex Rodriguez, and Albert Pujols in the early-to-mid 2000s—and, before that, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays, and Ernie Banks in the late 1950s and Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx, and Lou Gehrig in the early 1930s. But it’s also a product of the lowest-ever five-year average WAR tally for pitching pacers (6.4), with the exception of the pandemic-suppressed 2019 to 2023 period and a late-’50s stretch of historically lackluster leading arms.
The culprit isn’t much of a mystery: It’s the playing-time totals. Modern pitchers are working smarter, not harder. (Or, if we want to be charitable, similarly hard, but in shorter bursts.) Collectively, pitchers throw roughly the same number of innings as ever, and accrue just as much WAR. (FanGraphs allots 1,000 WAR leaguewide per season, with 57 percent going to hitters and 43 percent apportioned to pitchers.) But those innings and WAR are distributed across many more arms than they used to be, as innings eating nears extinction and the starting-pitcher protagonist of the past fades from view. Modern major leaguers’ workload diminution is much more apparent for pitchers than hitters. The chart below shows the number of hitters and pitchers who qualified for the batting title and ERA title, respectively, in each season of MLB’s 30-team era (since 1998, excluding 2020). The height of the bars (blue for hitters, orange for pitchers) indicates the number of qualifying players; the numbers above each bar (which could still increase slightly for 2026) denote the average number of plate appearances or innings within each year’s qualifying cohort.
Matt Olson aside, hitters aren’t totally immune to load management. Relative to the late 1990s, the number of qualifying hitters per season has sunk by about 15 percent, and the average number of plate appearances among qualifying hitters has been trimmed by a couple percent. But that’s nothing compared to the cratering of pitcher playing time. The number of qualifying pitchers per season has plummeted by nearly 50 percent, and the average number of innings among the remaining qualifiers has dropped by upwards of 10 percent.
Hence the ho-hum WAR totals mustered of late by baseball’s best pitchers, in an era of familiarity-effect avoidance, rampant pitcher injuries and, relatedly, an increased emphasis on max-effort throwing. As dazzling as today’s top arms are on an inning-per-inning basis—especially fastball-slider monsters like Mason Miller, whose outings are mostly contained to one frame—their GIFable filth comes at a cost. They can’t have both blistering stuff and exceptional staying power.
There’s no perfect substitute for the bulk starters used to supply. In 2019, for instance, Astros starter Gerrit Cole broke J.R. Richard’s single-season franchise record for strikeouts, 40 years after Richard’s nasty 1979 campaign. That accomplishment led to a sentimental meeting on the mound between past and present Astros aces, less than two years before Richard’s death. But although Cole surpassed Richard’s strikeout total, he couldn’t match his complete contribution: Richard threw 80 more innings, and recorded 8.9 WAR to Cole’s 7.5. Even Cole’s 212 1/3 innings in 2019 would be a standout total today; beyond Burnes in 2021, no pitcher since Cole has broken the 7-WAR wall.
On a long enough timescale, almost everything in sports circles back around. Someday, new rules might restore the starter’s lost luster, or overdue expansion might lower the major league replacement level and make the most competent pitchers look like WARlords again. League-leading hitters of the 2020s may be mogging their pitching counterparts when we focus on the DH era, but if we go back to the beginning of the National League, when hurlers who threw 400, 500, or 600 innings ruled the roost, we spot two subsequent stretches when the best bats had it even better than they do now: that late-’50s, offense-friendly low ebb for aces, and the 1920s and early ’30s, when Babe Ruth reinvented offense and broke baseball’s value scale. Once upon a time (or two), this batter-pitcher imbalance wasn’t so strange.
For now, though, we seem to be stuck in a phase where the cream of the crop of pitchers pales in comparison to elite everyday dudes. The sinking ceiling of starting-pitcher value may have implications for how pitchers are paid and staffs are assembled (not to mention how prospects are hyped). Free-agent pitchers make as much money per win as free-agent hitters, but if teams start expecting fewer wins from star pitchers than they do from star hitters, even the scarcity of healthy ligaments might not keep pitcher contracts from shrinking (and dragging down overall player pay). From the fan perspective, though, the more relevant byproduct of this modern mismatch in the value of leading hitters and pitchers is a shift in how we experience and describe standout seasons.
Because hitter playing-time totals today are comparable to what they were a century ago, we can still celebrate league-leading hitters via counting stats alone. We can convey his greatness just by marveling at how many homers he’s hit and bases he’s swiped; “the first 40-40 center fielder” would sound spiffy. If we want to dig deeper, we could note that only Triple Crown contender Yordan Alvarez stands in the way of PCA becoming the first player ever to lead the majors in both batting and fielding value in a single season, which would be a two-way feat almost as mind-blowing as Shohei Ohtani’s pitching/hitting heroics. At peak pitch speed, he’s the hardest-throwing starter on record (and in all likelihood, ever), and damn near the hardest-throwing pitcher, period.
In a sense, the Miz is just as impactful as PCA—he just hasn’t had as many chances to make an impact. PCA has paired his 702 trips to the plate (offensive chances, essentially) with 380 chances in center, for a grand total of 1,082 opportunities to determine the outcome of a plate appearance. Misiorowski has faced 646 batters, or 60 percent of PCA’s combined plate appearances plus defensive chances. If we look at things that way—i.e., by doing dubious addition—then the Miz has done well to accumulate 63 percent of PCA’s WAR.
Plus, in defense of Misiorowski and the constellation of starters who trail him by 1 WAR or less—AL Cy Young lock Cam Schlittler, Cristopher Sánchez, Chris Sale, Jesús Luzardo, and Dylan Cease—the tale of the 2026 WAR leader is as much about Crow-Armstrong vs. the field as it is pitchers vs. hitters. Only Ohtani and Witt sit between PCA and Misiorowski on FanGraphs’ WAR leaderboard, and both only barely lead the Miz. WAR is always subject to retroactive updates, but if none of the players clustered between 6.4 and 6.7 WAR—Ohtani, Misiorowski, Witt, and Alvarez—finishes strong, this could be the first unabridged season since 1950 (when teams played 154 games) in which MLB’s second-most-valuable player doesn’t touch 7 WAR. Fittingly, the AL’s MVP contenders are as underwhelming as the AL’s contending teams.
“Underwhelming” doesn’t describe Misiorowski. Of course, the quality that makes the Miz so awe-inspiring—he throws hard enough to remove a mortal’s arm from its socket—is also what makes him so anxiety-inducing. It’s not as if hitters can’t get hurt by running, throwing, or swinging hard—or even by standing somewhere in the vicinity of the on-deck circle, as Crow-Armstrong’s teammate Alex Bregman (whose WAR total since the All-Star break is exceeded only by PCA’s) painfully learned on Sunday. But they aren’t as prone to season-ending disaster as a matter of routine.
We delight in PCA’s uninhibited, prolific play, while we watch the Miz’s impressive but sparing appearances through splayed fingers. As Joe Posnanski pointed out in July, pitching might be the only assignment in sports where “simply doing your job is so scary and treacherous.” Not because an opposing player might flatten you, or because you might, say, stumble and get sliced by a skate blade, but because the fundamental motion endemic to your duty is hazardous to your health. Which helps explain why teams have sought to limit how often pitchers perform that motion, for all the good it’s done them. As it turns out, making that motion more dangerous but doing it less doesn’t make UCLs safer.
Misiorowski has survived the season with only minor, sporadic complaints: a hamstring cramp here, a dead arm there. To forestall more serious trouble, and to preserve their most prized pitcher for the postseason, the Brewers have handled him carefully. Since the All-Star Game (which he missed), he’s tied for 72nd in innings pitched, with two pitchers (Jack Perkins and Zebby Matthews) who have matching 4.94 ERAs over that span. But in October, when off days allow for compression of a pitching staff, an unrestrained Miz may emerge to shoulder more of Milwaukee’s workload and make overmatched opponents and concerned spectators alike quake like Ralph Wiggum. Over a season, or even a series, a position player such as PCA may amass more value. But in any given game, an ace can still slay.

title: 부상 악재 이정후, 사실상 시즌 아웃
author: 국제신문
body:
|  | 
| 샌프란시스코 자이언츠 이정후가 지난 19일(한국시간) 미국에서 열린 LA 다저스와의 경기에서 2회 초 홈런을 치고 있다.AFP 연합뉴스 | 
이정후(샌프란시스코 자이언츠)가 정규시즌 마무리를 코 앞에 두고 부상자 명단에 올라 시즌을 일찍 마감했다.
미국프로야구 메이저리그(MLB) 샌프란시스코는 22일(한국시간) 이정후를 열흘짜리 부상자 명단(IL)에 올린다고 밝혔다. 샌프란시스코는 22일 기준 정규시즌 마무리까지 5경기를 남겨두고 있고, 내셔널리그 서부지구 4위(승률 0.414·65승 92패)에 그쳐 포스트시즌 경쟁에서 탈락했다. 이에 따라 이정후는 열흘 뒤 복귀하더라도 올 시즌 남은 경기에 출전하기 어렵다.
이정후는 지난 21일 미국 캘리포니아주 로스앤젤레스 다저스타디움에서 열린 LA 다저스와의 원정 경기에서 6회 초 자신의 타구에 사타구니를 맞았다. 이후 경기를 이어갔으나 결국 7회 말 수비를 앞두고 교체됐다. 이후 검진에서 휴식이 필요한 타박상 진단을 받았다.
이정후는 이날까지 세 경기 연속 안타를 치는 등 상승세를 타고 있었기에 아쉬움이 크다. 그는 올 시즌 143경기에 출전해 타율 0.276 539타수 149안타(10홈런) 57타점 65득점 12도루를 기록해 2024년 MLB 데뷔 후 타율·홈런·타점·도루 부문에서 가장 좋은 성적을 기록했다.
이정후는 올 시즌 중반 17경기 연속 안타를 터뜨리며 MLB에 진출한 한국 타자 가운데 ‘최장 연속 경기 안타’ 기록을 세우는 등 승승장구했다. 당시 매서운 타격감을 뽐내며 리그 타율 선두 경쟁을 다퉜으나 시즌 후반 주춤하면서 아쉬운 성적으로 마무리하게 됐다.

title: 【ＭＬＢ】ケガに泣かされた吉田正尚「球団の忍耐も限界に近づいている」ＰＳ出場も望み薄＝米報道 | 東スポWEB
author: 東スポWeb
body:
レッドソックスの吉田正尚外野手（３３）が厳しい状況を迎えている。現在も左足ハムストリングの負傷で故障者リスト入りしており、ポストシーズンのロースター入りも望み薄。ＭＬＢ４年目の今季もケガに悩まされて８７試合で打率２割７分４厘、５本塁打、２８打点にとどまり、結果を出せなかった。吉田をめぐっては何度となく放出の噂があったが、そのたびに５年９０００万ドル（約１４２億円）の高額契約が足かせとなって移籍には至らなかったとされる。
しかし、今シーズンも期待を裏切り、契約期間が来年まで続くことを思えば球団の我慢も限界。米メディア「アルバット」は「吉田はまさに時限爆弾だ。かつてフロントの最も大胆な賭けの１つと見られたこの日本人スターは度重なるケガとその真の実力に対する疑問に悩まされてきた。彼は現在も故障者リスト入りし、プレーオフのロースター入りも疑問符だ」と切り捨てている。
さらに「２０２７年まで年俸１８００万ドル（約２８億円）を受け取る彼は、長打力も守備力もない指名打者だ。特に外野争いが激化している現状では正当化しがたいぜいたく品だ。フロントは彼を放出するために契約のかなりの部分を負担しなければならないだろうが、忍耐も限界に近づいている」と見ている。状態さえよければ非凡な打撃力を発揮できるが、今や球団の信頼を取り戻すのは難しい。
地元メディア「ボソックス・インジェクション」も「レッドソックスのユニホームを着て最後の時を過ごす選手」として紹介し「彼がプレーオフのロースター入りに値しない理由はあまりに多い。どうフィットするのか想像しにくい」と報じている。

title: MLB roundup: Pete Alonso hits HRs 39, 40 as Orioles top Jays
body:
Pete Alonso’s second home run of the game and 40th of the season lifted the Baltimore Orioles to a 4-3 comeback victory against the visiting Toronto Blue Jays in the opener of a three-game series Monday night.
Alonso’s two-run shot with two outs in the eighth inning gave Baltimore its first lead of the game. The Orioles pulled within 4 1/2 games of the White Sox in the race for the third American League wild card, while the Blue Jays now trail Chicago by 3 1/2 games.
Alonso also homered in the first inning and Gunnar Henderson (3-for-4) went deep in the sixth inning as the Orioles ended a three-game losing streak. Baltimore reliever Yennier Cano (4-3) worked 1 1/3 shutout innings, and Rico Garcia pitched a 1-2-3 ninth for his 10th save.
George Springer had two singles and an RBI for the Blue Jays, who lost for the fifth time in seven games. Tyler Rogers (2-3) gave up the decisive home run.
Tigers 9, Nationals 2
Ben Malgeri hit a three-run home run, Javier Baez and Spencer Torkelson each supplied two-run shots and host Detroit opened a three-game series with a romp over Washington.
River Ryan, elevated from Triple-A, started and pitched three scoreless innings while recording three strikeouts in his Tigers debut. Ryan, acquired in August from the Dodgers in the Tarik Skubal deal, last pitched in the majors in 2024. Keider Montero (10-9) followed with four shutout innings while striking out five.
Pinch hitter Yohandy Morales produced a two-run homer for the Nationals, who took their second loss in a row. DJ Herz (0-1) allowed four runs in four innings during his first major league outing since 2024.
Giants 5, Twins 2
Drew Gilbert homered, collected three hits and drove in a career-high-tying three runs as host San Francisco defeated Minnesota.
Brett Harris chipped in two hits, including a two-run single, as the Giants snapped a three-game losing streak. San Francisco reliever Tristan Beck (1-0) threw 2 2/3 innings of hitless ball, and Trent Harris tossed a perfect ninth inning for his second save.
Brooks Lee and Emmanuel Rodriguez homered for the Twins, who lost for the sixth time in nine games. Zebby Matthews (9-11) fanned nine in five innings but yielded five runs on eight hits.
–Field Level Media

title: Gunnar Henderson goes 3-for-4, homers in win
author: George Bissell; Gunnar Henderson
body:
Gunnar Henderson went 3-for-4 with his 24th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays.
            
                Henderson’s three-hit effort included a solo homer off Toronto rookie reliever Chad Dallas as he finished a double shy of hitting for the cycle. It’s been a down year relative to expectations for Henderson, especially in the stolen base department where he has just 10 thefts after reaching the 30-steal mark last year.

title: 이정후, 사타구니 타박상으로 부상자명단에 이름 올려… 타율 0.276으로 시즌 마감
author: 이소연
body:
샌프란시스코 구단은 22일 “이정후가 10일짜리 부상자명단(IL)에 이름을 올렸다. 복귀 예상 시기는 2027년”이라고 알렸다. 
이정후는 하루 전 LA 다저스와의 방문경기 6회초 세 번째 타석에서 파울 타구에 사타구니 쪽을 맞고 7회 드류 길버트(26)와 교체됐다. 
이날 현재 64승 92패로 내셔널리그 서부지구 4위에 처져있는 샌프란시스코는 포스트시즌 진출이 무산됐다. 이로써 이정후의 MLB 세 번째 시즌이 조기에 끝난 셈이다.
            이정후는 올 시즌 143경기에 출전해 타율 0.276, 10홈런, 57타점, 12도루, OPS(출루율+장타율) 0.724를 남겼다. 
타율은 지난 시즌(0.266)보다 1푼 올랐지만 OPS는 0.010 떨어졌다.
6월 한때 MLB 타율 2위까지 올랐지만 7, 8월 타율이 2할대에 그치며 3할을 사수하지 못했다. 
이정후는 이달 17경기에선 타율 0.188(64타수 12안타)을 기록 중이었다. 
이정후마저 부상을 당하면서 샌프란시스코는 올 시즌 개막전 선발 명단에 이름을 올린 야수 9명이 모두 부상과 트레이드로 전력에서 이탈했다.

title: Alex Bregman sufre múltiples fracturas tras ser golpeado por bola, pero descartan cirugía
body:
El fin de semana, el jugador de los Chicago Cubs, Alex Bregman, tuvo que abandonar el juego ante los Cincinnati Reds, luego de que recibió un fuerte pelotazo en el rostro mientras estaba esperando su turno al bat.
La situación parece ser más grave de lo que se esperaba, luego de que se dio a conocer un diagnóstico sobre el tercera base de los Cachorros, quien mostró las huellas de la batalla en sus redes sociales.
RECOMENDAMOS: Selección Mexicana jugaría en estadio de Rayados la Nations League; volverían a Monterrey tras 8 años
¿Qué tan grave es la lesión de Alex Bregman?
De acuerdo con información de Jeff Passan de ESPN, la lesión sí es complicada, pues se dice que Alex Bregman sufrió múltiples fracturas en la cara, algo que será complicado para el equipo de los Chicago Cubs.
A pesar de que la lesión es mucho más importante de lo que se esperaba, también hay buenas noticias, puesto que no se espera que el jugador vaya a ser sometido a una cirugía.
¿Cuándo podría regresar Alex Bregman a los campos?
Aunque no está conformado por la gente de los Chicago Cubs, la misma fuente dio a conocer que se espera que Alex Bregman pueda regresar esta misma temporada para el momento más importante, la postemporada.
Hay que recordar que el jugador que ocupa la tercera base de los Cubs tuvo que ser enviado al hospital para evaluar la situación del golpe que recibió en el juego del domingo.
Por otra parte, el propio Alex Bregman se ha encargado de compartir algunas fotos de cómo le quedó la cara después del bolazo que lo dejará fuera en la recta final de la temporada regular de la MLB.

title: Claros favoritos en la última encuesta del JMV, pero ¿podrá esta semana cambiar algo?
author: Brian Murphy
body:
Mientras marchamos por la última semana de la temporada regular, no parece haber mucho suspenso respecto a quiénes serán nombrados JMV. Al menos, eso es lo que podemos descifrar de nuestra más reciente -- y última -- encuesta del JMV de MLB.com para el 2026.
El cubano Yordan Álvarez sigue estando bien al frente en la Liga Americana a pesar de una producción relativamente mediocre recientemente. En la Liga Nacional, Pete Crow-Armstrong está cerrando una de las mejores campañas completas en tiempos recientes.
Treinta y ocho expertos de MLB.com emitieron sus votos sobre quiénes creen que se llevarán los honores de JMV tras esta temporada, con 32 jugadores recibiendo al menos un voto. Como recordatorio, los votos se basaron no solo en el desempeño hasta ahora, sino también en cómo se espera que evolucionen las cosas durante el resto de la campaña.
Los votantes clasificaron a sus cinco principales candidatos de cada liga con un sistema de 5-4-3-2-1: cinco puntos por un voto al primer lugar, cuatro por el segundo, y así sucesivamente. Estos son los resultados.
Todas las estadísticas son hasta la jornada del domingo, a menos que se indique lo contrario.
LIGA AMERICANA
Álvarez ha tenido un desempeño tan bueno este año que lo que califica como un bache para él sería un gran trecho para la mayoría de los demás bateadores. En sus últimos 41 encuentros, batea .264 con OPS de .840. Reiteramos, nada mal para la mayoría, pero muy por debajo del nivel del líder de la Americana en promedio (.313) y OPS (1.027). Álvarez lleva tres cuadrangulares y cinco impulsadas a lo largo de 16 partidos este mes, dejándolo a un jonrón del dominicano Junior Caminero de los Rays por el liderato en el Joven Circuito y a seis empujadas de Pete Alonso por la cima en dicho departamento. Aunque sus posibilidades de la Triple Corona se están desvaneciendo un poco, Álvarez todavía ha armado un 2026 asombroso en el plato. Su wRC+ de 179 es al menos 27 puntos mejor que el de cualquier otro bateador calificado.
Sabemos que el quisqueyano es uno de los grandes cañoneros del juego. Está cerrando su segunda temporada consecutiva de 40 vuelacercas y está dando swings más fuerte que nadie. Pero lo que ha sido más impresionante de su temporada es su mejorado criterio en la zona de strike. Aumentó su tasa de boletos desde un 6.3% por debajo del promedio a un 11.5%, lo que se ubica en el 80mo percentil de MLB. También ha mantenido una tasa de ponches muy sólida (18.5%). Ya no persigue tantos pitcheos fuera de la zona, ha reducido su tasa de swings en blanco y está haciendo más contacto en general. Esa mezcla de paciencia, trueno y control del bate es una combinación especial, sobre todo en un jugador de 23 años. Luciendo un porcentaje de embasarse de .363 (52 puntos mejor que la campaña pasada), el OPS de .892 de Caminero se ubica tercero en la Americana.
Witt ha tenido mejores campañas a la ofensiva, aunque 18 bambinazos, 43 estafadas y wRC+ de 119 en 137 partidos no está nada mal. Pero cuando se consideran todas sus capacidades, Witt sigue siendo extremadamente valioso. Su valor de carreras defensivas de +16 está empatado en el tercer lugar de las Grandes Ligas, y sus 22 outs por encima del promedio encabezan la Liga Americana. También cuenta con un valor de carreras en el corrido de bases de +8, a uno de Corbin Carroll de los Diamondbacks por el liderato de MLB. Por eso, aunque no ha sido tan indiscutible en la caja de bateo como lo fue en el 2024 (wRC+ de 169), la grandeza integral de Witt lo tiene en la cima de la tabla de posiciones de WAR de FanGraphs en el Joven Circuito (6.6) y posiblemente perfilándolo entre los primeros cinco en la votación para JMV por tercera vez en tres años.
Ha habido bastante conversación de JMV entorno a Schlittler en las últimas semanas. ¿Y por qué no? Está marcando el paso en la Americana en efectividad (1.94), WHIP (0.91) y WAR de pitcheo de FanGraphs (6.1). Se ubica segundo en el Joven Circuito en promedio de bateo en contra (.182) y en tasa de ponches menos boletos (25.0%). Ha permitido una carrera o ninguna en 21 aperturas. Ese es un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees y algo que apenas otros dos lanzadores de 25 años o menos han logrado en la Era de la Pelota Viva (desde 1920): Blake Snell (2018) y Dean Chance (1964). Seguramente será reconocido con el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana a estas alturas, pero Schlittler recibirá su merecida cuota de consideración para el JMV.
Schlittler no ha sido el único miembro de los Bombarderos que ha sido indispensable este año. Mientras Nueva York ha estado sin Aaron Judge durante una gran parte de la campaña y ha echado de menos a otros bates estelares debido a lesiones, Rice ha sido demostrado consistencia. Nadie tiene más anotadas (118), extrabases (83) o total de bases anotadas (351) esta campaña. Con 38 estafadas, el dinámico jardinero central del equipo del Norte de Chicago podría convertirse en el séptimo miembro del club 40-40 más adelante esta semana. No lanzará por el resto de la temporada, dejándolo con efectividad de 1.79 y 95 ponches en 85.2 entradas. Mencionamos antes cómo Schlittler luce como el gran favorito para el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Misiorowski tendría su premio más asegurado en la Nacional. A lo largo de 169.1 episodios, Miz encabeza la Gran Carpa en casi cada categoría, incluyendo efectividad (1.86), WHIP (0.80), tasa de ponches menos boletos (31.7%) y fWAR (6.5), por nombrar solo algunas.
