title: A piece of advice we want the next NY Mets voices to give David Stearns
author: Pat Ragazzo
body:
New York Mets owner Steve Cohen made it clear to the team's broadcast booth in a recent interview that the organization intends on bringing in some new voices to the front office this offseason. That's because president of baseball operations David Stearns and the current regime had a poor year in 2026.
"We're going to try to add certain voices into the front office that I think will be helpful," Cohen said. "I know David supports that and I'm looking forward to, when we make those decisions, announcing it."
While it would make sense for the Mets to bring in a general manager to work as Stearns' No. 2, Cohen said that doesn't necessarily need to be the case.
"It doesn't have to be a GM," Cohen said. "It could be other ways to support David and the front office."
So, whether it's a GM or not, the Mets will be bringing in new perspectives this winter to assist Stearns and the front office. And once that happens, here's the advice this new voice/s should give Stearns and co.
Advice to Mets baseball head honcho David Stearns
This should be an easy one as it was Stearns' biggest blunder of the year; Don't rely on injury prone/aging players. Stearns brought in the likes of Jorge Polanco, Luis Robert Jr. and Marcus Semien as new faces to replace franchise mainstays: Pete Alonso, Brandon Nimmo and Jeff McNeil.
This strategy proved to be a big mistake given all three new acquisitions missed time due to injury this year and greatly underperformed. Not to mention, the trio Stearns let go of all play everyday and rarely miss time each year. The new GM or voice/s should be advising Stearns to re-evaluate how he views durability/reliability when it comes to player acquisition. Polanco and Robert already had reputations for being injury prone in their careers.
The Mets cannot go into another season relying on Polanco to play first base (coming off ankle surgery) or Semien (36-years-old) to play second base. Both players are making a good bit of money next season, but the Mets shouldn't force them to be full-time players when they aren't reliable. Robert was claimed off waivers by the Baltimore Orioles, so the Mets are no longer on the hook for his $2 million buyout.
The new voice/s should be helping Stearns pull off creative trades and find low-risk, high-reward veteran options that can produce for the Mets next season. The Mets had the second-highest payroll in baseball behind the Los Angeles Dodgers, but had a disastrous year. It clearly makes sense for them to bring some new voices into the fold for next season and beyond.

rss_title: A piece of advice we want the next NY Mets voices to give David Stearns
rss_body:
New York Mets owner Steve Cohen made it clear to the team's broadcast booth in a recent interview that the organization intends on bringing in some new voices to the front office this offseason. That's because president of baseball operations David Stearns and the current regime had a poor year in 2026.
"We're going to try to add certain voices into the front office that I think will be helpful," Cohen said. "I know David supports that and I'm looking forward to, when we make those decisions, announcing it."
While it would make sense for the Mets to bring in a general manager to work as Stearns' No. 2, Cohen said that doesn't necessarily need to be the case.
"It doesn't have to be a GM," Cohen said. "It could be other ways to support David and the front office."
So, whether it's a GM or not, the Mets will be bringing in new perspectives this winter to assist Stearns and the front office. And once that happens, here's the advice this new voice/s should give Stearns and co.
Advice to Mets baseball head honcho David Stearns
This should be an easy one as it was Stearns' biggest blunder of the year; Don't rely on injury prone/aging players. Stearns brought in the likes of Jorge Polanco, Luis Robert Jr. and Marcus Semien as new faces to replace franchise mainstays: Pete Alonso, Brandon Nimmo and Jeff McNeil.
This strategy proved to be a big mistake given all three new acquisitions missed time due to injury this year and greatly underperformed. Not to mention, the trio Stearns let go of all play everyday and rarely miss time each year. The new GM or voice/s should be advising Stearns to re-evaluate how he views durability/reliability when it comes to player acquisition. Polanco and Robert already had reputations for being injury prone in their careers.
The Mets cannot go into another season relying on Polanco to play first base (coming off ankle surgery) or Semien (36-years-old) to play second base. Both players are making a good bit of money next season, but the Mets shouldn't force them to be full-time players when they aren't reliable. Robert was claimed off waivers by the Baltimore Orioles, so the Mets are no longer on the hook for his $2 million buyout.
The new voice/s should be helping Stearns pull off creative trades and find low-risk, high-reward veteran options that can produce for the Mets next season. The Mets had the second-highest payroll in baseball behind the Los Angeles Dodgers, but had a disastrous year. It clearly makes sense for them to bring some new voices into the fold for next season and beyond.

title: SF Giants add Mayer, Davidson as Eldridge, Lee land on injured list
author: Justice Delos Santos
body:
SAN FRANCISCO — First, the good news: outfielder Bo Davidson and infielder Marcelo Mayer will make their long-awaited Giants debuts on Monday night at Oracle Park against the Minnesota Twins. Now, the bad: Bryce Eldridge and Jung Hoo Lee became the latest players to hit the injured list.
Mayer, acquired at the trade deadline from the Boston Red Sox, was reinstated from the injured list, while Davidson was called up from Triple-A Sacramento. Davidson will play right field and bat third in his major-league debut, while Mayer will bat fourth and be the team’s designated hitter.
“Just showing them what I can do and giving them the best I can every game until the season’s over,” Davidson said when asked what he could provide. “Just showing them what Bo is.”
What is Bo?
“You’ll see,” Davidson said with a smile.
Meanwhile, Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion list after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles, while Lee landed on the 10-day injured list with a groin contusion after fouling a ball off himself on Sunday. Lee’s season is over, and manager Tony Vitello said he doesn’t anticipate Eldridge will play again this season, which ends Sunday.
With Lee landing on the injured list, every member of the Opening Day lineup is either on the injured list (Lee, Willy Adames, Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt, Harrison Bader) or has been traded (Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez). The only players from the Opening Day roster still on the roster are infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp.
Adames (left elbow sprain) took grounders and batting practice on Monday afternoon, but he’s very unlikely to return before the end of the season.
Eldridge, who will turn 22 next month, exceeded expectations as a rookie and should be a foundational piece of the Giants’ lineup alongside Devers. Over 107 games, Eldridge hit .269/.364/.461 with 17 home runs, 23 doubles and 57 RBIs. Among rookies, Eldridge’s 130 wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) was the third-highest in the majors.
“Incredibly impressive,” Vitello said of Eldridge’s season. “We summarized that a little bit with him this morning in there. Maturity is the word that gets thrown around a bunch, but it got thrown around in there, too. I think consistency is the other word. He attached that to himself in a good way, not in a braggadocious way.
“If I could speak for him through his own words, a big difference between last year and this year is understanding the ups and downs and how to maintain consistency, which is a lot easier to formulate or plan out than it is to put into act.”
Along with the offense, Vitello also highlighted Eldridge’s defense, which was his biggest question as a prospect. After committing 18 errors in 2024 and 9 in 2025, Eldridge only had two errors this season in the majors and minors. Eldridge also graded out well by Baseball Savant’s new first baseman receiving metric.
Going into next season, one area where Vitello believes Eldridge can improve is baserunning.
“He’s got good instincts, but there’s so many things that he’s seeing for the first time in his life, literally,” Vitello said. “Safety bunts, stuff like that. And then on the base running … he didn’t do anything that would cause us to jump here in the dugout or cost us big, but for a guy that’s going to be on base as often as he is — and he’s not a burner — he’s got to be good on those little separators of reads, preparation before a pitch.”
Davidson, 24, is the Giants’ No. 5 prospect, per Baseball America. Over 125 games this season with Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, Davidson hit .290 with 29 home runs, 20 steals and 94 RBIs. He was a candidate to get called up earlier this month but missed a week after fouling a ball off his foot on Sept. 9.
For all of Davidson’s production on the field, he believes the biggest area he’s grown has been “being a better man off the field.”
Davidson is one of many intriguing prospects in a farm system that has climbed the rankings. Along with Davidson, the Giants’ farm system is headlined by shortstops Josuar Gonzalez and Luis Hernandez, as well as right-handed pitcher Jackson Flora.
“We’ve got a very special group of guys that’s coming through,” said Davidson, whose mother, brother, girlfriend and daughter will be in attendance. “The farm itself, the numbers this year just showed. Us being really good brothers off the field, it just shows on the field with the chemistry.”
“I’m excited to see Bo again,” Vitello said. “Just kind of knowing who he was in high school and junior college. … We were able to get him some action in spring training, and then you’re following along, following along. We knew [his promotion] would happen at some point.”
Mayer, 23, was traded to the Giants on Aug. 3 from the Boston Red Sox in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor-league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. The infielder had been recovering from a bone stress reaction to the left ulna, as well as a bone bruise on his right foot.
Vitello anticipates Mayer will primarily be the team’s designated hitter over the final six games, but he could also see some time in the infield.

title: Juan Soto Joins Elite Club With 270 Homers, 100 Stolen Bases Before 28th Birthday
author: J Mayhew
body:
Juan Soto Joins Elite Club With 270 Homers, 100 Stolen Bases Before 28th Birthday
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the…
Juan Soto of the New York Mets hits a double in the second inning against the Philadelphia Phillies at Citi Field on September 18, 2026 in New York City.
Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images
New York Mets outfielder Juan Soto just became the fourth player in MLB history to hit 270 home runs and steal 100 bases before his 28th birthday. Friday night, the 27-year-old crushed a 428-foot three-run blast against the Philadelphia Phillies.
Who else made this list? Alex Rodriguez, Ken Griffey Jr., and Mike Trout, per MLB's Sarah Langs. Every player in this group debuted at 19.
According to Essentially Sports, Soto went 3-for-5 with one homer, 3 RBIs, and a run scored against Philadelphia. He's up to 26 homers in 103 games despite missing time on the injured list twice this year.
The five-time All-Star needed 1,199 MLB games to reach 270 home runs. He's also collected 210 doubles as part of his 1,187 hits.
The Dominican star has swiped 104 bases in 134 tries. Last season, he stole 38 bags—a massive jump from his previous career-high of just 12. This year he's 9-for-12 on the basepaths.
Soto draws walks like few others can. He's led MLB in walks four times and has six seasons with at least 100 free passes. Career totals? 969 walks versus only 893 strikeouts. Among active players, he leads everyone with a .415 on-base percentage.
New York inked the outfielder as a free agent before the 2025 season. His contract: 15 years, $765 million. That's the biggest deal in MLB history.
The Mets sit in last place in the NL East at 70-84. Many experts predicted they'd contend for the division title this year. They haven't.
Soto's still producing. He's batting .274 with a .920 OPS across 444 plate appearances in 103 games. His season started late on April 22 after he recovered from a right calf strain. Then he hit the IL again in late July with a left calf strain. He earned his fifth All-Star selection this season but didn't play in the game.

title: ‘사타구니 부상’ 이정후, 10일짜리 IL…사실상 ‘시즌아웃’
author: 오해원 기자
body:
미국프로야구 메이저리그(MLB) 샌프란시스코 자이언츠의 주전 외야수 이정후가 불의의 부상을 당해 올해 잔여 일정에 출전할 수 없게 됐다.
샌프란시스코 구단은 22일(한국시간) 이정후가 열흘짜리 부상자 명단(IL)에 올랐다고 발표했다.
이정후는 지난 21일 로스앤젤레스 다저스와 원정경기 중 자신의 타수에 사타구니를 맞았다. 사고 직후 교체된 이정후는 경기 후 검진에서 휴식이 필요한 타박상 진단을 받았다.
현재 64승92패로 내셔널리그 서부지구 4위인 샌프란시스코는 포스트시즌 진출이 무산됐고, 정규시즌 6경기가 남았다. 이정후가 복귀할 시점에는 모든 경기가 종료되는 만큼 이번 부상은 시즌 아웃이나 다름없다.
이정후는 2026 MLB에서 143경기에 출전해 타율 0.276, 10홈런, 57타점, 65득점, 12도루, 출루율 0.320, 장타율 0.404를 남겼다.
타율과 홈런, 타점, 도루는 2024시즌 MLB에 진출한 뒤 가장 좋은 성적이다. 특히 시즌 중반에는 타격 순위 최상위권을 다툴 정도로 경기력이 좋았으나 막판에는 흐름이 꺾여 아쉬움을 남겼다. 하지만 출루율과 장타율은 지난해보다 하락했다.

title: Paul Skenes culpa al Clásico Mundial por su bajo rendimiento en la MLB
author: Editorial Mediotiempo
body:
Los señalamientos sobre la temporalidad del Clásico Mundial de Béisbol han vuelto a crear controversia en la MLB, especialmente por los comentarios de Paul Skenes, el Novato del Año en 2024 y ganador del Premio Cy Young en 2025 dentro de la Liga Nacional, quien apuntó al torneo como responsable sobre su bajo desempeño, disminuyendo su velocidad y empeorando su efectividad.
¿Qué dijo Paul Skenes del Clásico Mundial?
“Hay un montón de factores, así que no quiero poner toda la responsabilidad en eso”, dijo Skenes el fin de semana al Post-Gazette de Pittsburgh. “Pero siento que esa fue, un poco, la raíz de todo el asunto”.
El Clásico Mundial ha sido constantemente señalado por su temporalidad respecto a la temporada de las Grandes Ligas. Celebrándose durante los entrenamientos primaverales de cada tres o cuatro años, los peloteros a veces acusan que el torneo les exige un máximo esfuerzo cuando apenas están terminando su preparación luego de cinco meses de receso invernal.
Paul Skenes on the World Baseball Classic and its impact on his velocity and effectiveness this season, via @colin_beazley:
"There are a lot of other factors, so I don’t want to put everything on that. But I feel like that was kind of the root of it a little bit."
"It… pic.twitter.com/wHZ002GU9O
Skenes apenas lanzó 8.1 entradas y solamente admitió una carrera para ayudar a Estados Unidos a llegar a la gran final. Paul ganó sus dos aperturas mostrando un gran control con 9 ponches y solo una base por bolas.
Al principio de la temporada, Skenes dijo que la disminución de su velocidad era intencional. Con el paso de sus aperturas, las semanas y los meses, Skenes tuvo que admitir que no sabía exactamente qué había pasado.
Ahora, Skenes tiene una respuesta contundente.
Rafael Devers takes Paul Skenes to deep center for a three-run shot! pic.twitter.com/FHLSnUmYlN
— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) September 1, 2026
“Regularmente, en esa época del año, te estás preparando (para la temporada) y el proceso suele ser un poco lento. Puedes, en cierto modo, adentrarte en la pendiente y encontrar tu ritmo”, agregó Skenes. “En una práctica puedes estar rozando las 97 mph y la siguiente estás tirando 98 o 99 mph. Y ese no fue mi caso este año”.
Paul Skenes, venido a menos tras el Clásico Mundial
El vigente ganador del Premio Cy Young tiene una efectividad de 3.91 esta temporada, casi dos carreras más que el 1.97 de carreras admitidas que promedió durante la temporada anterior. Su velocidad ha bajado y su comando se ha perdido.
Su poderosa recta, que en 2024 tuvo un promedio de 98.8 mph, según Statcast, un año después bajó a 98.1 mph y esta temporada cayó significativamente hasta promediar 96.8 mph.
The @Cubs get to Skenes and take a 3-run lead! pic.twitter.com/LE1tWKNEqU
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) July 26, 2026
“Cuando vas salida tras salida, a veces no ves el panorama completo. Y creo que, al mirar atrás, ahora sí puedo verlo”, dijo Skenes. “Porque al principio de la temporada puedes salir con algunos detalles en la mecánica o no moverte a la perfección; estás fresco y la velocidad está ahí porque te sientes bien. Pero eso no funciona en julio, agosto y septiembre”.
Un sector de la fanaticada comentó en redes sociales que los comentarios de Skenes parecen una campaña en contra del torneo, especialmente cuando existen casos de éxito de peloteros que participaron en el Clásico Mundial y están brillando en las Grandes Ligas.
El ejemplo más claro es el de Eduardo Rodríguez, que luego de ayudar a Venezuela a ganar el Clásico Mundial está teniendo el mejor año de su carrera al firmar una efectividad de 2.89 con los Diamondbacks antes de comenzar la última semana de la temporada regular; sus 15 juegos ganados es la mejor para él desde 2019.
Pese a la muestra, Skenes cree que no es el único afectado por el Clásico Mundial.
“Definitivamente afectó el año”, dijo Skenes. “Lamentablemente, no creo ser el único”.

title: FAAB Frenzy and Waivers Wild: Week 27
author: Vlad Sedler
body:
Every Monday, this column will break down the most popular waiver wire and free agent acquisitions from the weekend. I dig into the top adds on the ever-popular Fantrax and in the NFBC Online Championship (OC), a national mid-stakes contest with 240 total leagues of 12 and a six-figure grand prize. Reviewing player adds between the two should provide us with a well-rounded perspective and barometer of the fantasy baseball marketplace.
Week 26 Overview
Hitters
The San Diego Padres took advantage of their four-game series with the Rockies at Coors Field and a home set with the Marlins, scoring 51 runs, 12 more than any other team. Fernando Tatis Jr. (along with Brandon Lowe and Pete Crow-Armstrong) led the way with a week-high four dingers. Last week’s streamers turned out to be dynamite: Jake Cronenworth (.464-8-2-8-2), Dustin Harris (.379-5-0-7-2) and Samad Taylor (.556-6-1-7-1) really stepped up, particularly Taylor for my competitive Main Event squad that gained two category points in batting average last week. Rake Cronenworth was true to his nickname from several years ago. He led all Major League hitters with 13 hits. The Brewers swiped a league-high 12 bags last week: four each for Jackson Chourio and rookie Cooper Pratt. Tampa’s Chandler Simpson led all runners with five swipes, finally catching Washington’s Nasim Nuñez for the MLB lead with 46. Expect Simpson to finish with 50+ and win the stolen base crown.
Pitchers
Of the 29 two-start pitchers excluding Pirates opener Lake Bachar, three earned two wins: Tarik Skubal, Sean Burke and David Peterson. Houston’s Hunter Brown had an outstanding two-step (10 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 5 K – 20 K) and those 20 punchouts led all pitchers for the week. Gavin Williams punched out 16 in 12 innings and is back atop the AL lead in strikeouts with 244. Dylan Cease (239) may not make his final start of the season and Cam Schlittler (234) is unlikely to catch Williams as both have one start remaining. It’s very possible that Williams catches and passes Jacob Misiorowski (247) for the Major League lead. The Miz pitched three innings in his weekend start and might be limited for his final one.
Tampa’s Bryan Baker was the first reliever to reach 40 saves this season. It’s possible that Cade Smith (39), Riley O’Brien (38) and Mason Miller (37) join Baker. The last time there were three closers with 40 or more saves was in 2019: Edwin Díaz (57), Wade Davis (43), and Craig Kimbrel (42). Shout out to folks who drafted O’Brien late, and/or picked up Baker, Louis Varland or Jacob Latz off waivers and didn’t have to worry about the saves category all season.
Week 27 Most Added Players: NFBC Main Event, NFBC OC, and Fantrax
It’s the last hurrah for managers with FAB dollars left, hoping to get the best bang for the buck and for variance to lean their way and tip them into league titles. As is usually the case in the final week, we hope to optimize our pitching rotations and hitters in hitter-friendly ballparks against bad pitching. It was odd seeing Shohei Ohtani available in several leagues, and perhaps fortuitous as he should be activated this week and start a few games. Ohtani was acquired in 26 OCs for an AWB of $17. In Main Events, there were 12 shares available and they went for a reasonable $12 a pop. I scooped up a rare Ohtani share in an OC for $2, winning a tiebreaker over the team in 1st place in that league. Andy Pages will be activated on Tuesday, which should push Tommy Edman back to second base. Pages had been out since August 21, but was producing at an exciting clip before the injury — .272 – 72 R – 21 HR – 80 RBI – 12 SB in 550 PA. Managers who acquired him are hoping that he dusts the cobwebs back off and gets right into the swing of things, with all the marbles on the line.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 8 | Brayan Bello | BOS | SP | 35% | $11 | 
| 9 | Dustin Harris | SD | OF | 32% | $10 | 
| 10 | Garrett Whitlock | BOS | RP | 32% | $5 | 
| 11 | Pavin Smith | ARI | 1B | 30% | $4 | 
| 12 | Anthony Volpe | NYY | SS | 30% | $5 | 
AWB = Average Winning Bid (min: $4 AWB)
Pitchers were the most popular targets, specifically two-steppers, as we chase wins and strikeouts, hoping the Ratio Monster doesn’t eat our leads in ERA and WHIP. JR Ritchie and Daniel Lynch IV were the most added starters who we expect two starts from this week. Ritchie’s MLB debut back in April came with great promise, but walks haunted him greatly, which led to trips back to Triple-A to refine his craft and some bulk inning relief work when he returned to Atlanta in July. Ritchie was recently promoted again, and ran into a juggernaut Cubs offense last week, allowing six runs on seven hits in 4.2 innings. The walk rate (13.7%) isn’t pretty, and he has a good opportunity to end his season on a high note with two reasonable matchups — against the Reds at home and the Marlins on the road. Lynch had served the Royals well as their top southpaw out of the bullpen for most of the season. He moved to the rotation in August and slowly worked his pitch counts upward. Lynch has made it to five innings in each of his last three starts. His latest one (at HOU on September 16) went well — 5 IP – 2 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 3 K. More of that please as he faces the White Sox and Guardians at Kauffman Stadium in the final week. If I could only choose one for the week, it would be Ritchie.
Red Sox pitchers Brayan Bello and Garrett Whitlock were popular buys as the likelihood of roto stars shining bright on them this week is high. Bello is coming off a tremendous outing against the AL-leading Rays on Saturday where he posted an 11:0 K:BB with just one run allowed in eight innings. Those 11 punchies tied his career high. Bello had been the worst starter in the game (6.49 ERA, 1.67 WHIP) through June 4, when he was optioned to Triple-A. Since the All-Star break, mostly out of relief and with two starts, the 27-year-old has been shining. Over those 51.1 innings, he is rocking exemplary ratios (2.28 ERA, 1.01 WHIP) and a 17% K-BB% (22.3% K, 5.3% BB). Bello should make a start against the Cubs next Saturday. The Cubs should be settled into a playoff spot by then, so perhaps they give Pete Crow-Armstrong and some of the other regulars that day off. Boston’s closer Aroldis Chapman has been day-to-day with a lat issue, so perhaps the Red sox have him take it easy and provide Whitlock with some save opportunities. Whitlock has a 7-2 record with a 17.5 ERA, 0.88 WHIP and four saves.
Streaming Diamondbacks is a good idea this week, specifically for their three-game set at Coors Field against the Rockies in the early part of the week. Pavin Smith was a coveted target, coming off a four-day stretch where three of his hits were home runs. Don’t expect Smith to start against lefty Kyle Freeland, but he should be in the lineup for the other two contests against righties. Nolan Arenado was available in one of the 60 Main Event leagues and was acquired for just one dollar.
Better late than never for two punchless Padres who have been quite productive and certainly enjoyed their visit to Coors Field in the first half of last week. Dustin Harris ($10 AWB) and Samad Taylor ($5) have been red hot and playing often over the last 10 days. Though he doesn’t have a home run yet, Harris has been quite productive and helpful to early-bird managers: eight runs, 12 runs batted in and three steals, batting .384 with a 166 wRC+ in 40 plate appearances since September 11. He’s also been batting second against right-handed starters. Taylor has at least one hit in nine of his last 10, including a 3-for-3 effort on Sunday, and has driven in seven in his last seven games.

As always, more reliable starting pitcher depth was available in the 12-team OC pool. Cristian Javier, Anthony Kay, Robert Gasser, Lynch, Yusei Kikuchi, and Max Scherzer were the most added pitchers this week. Javier should pitch twice this week and will hope to put his best foot forward (in this case, his right arm) as the Astros fight for the AL West and a playoff spot. Sutter Health Park is not a fun place to pitch, but the A’s lineup is a watered-down version without Brent Rooker, Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, and Jacob Wilson윌슨. Javier’s first start is in Seattle may not be a picnic with gluten-free granola and Pearl Jam on the Discman.
Milwaukee’s Robert Gasser only draws one start (home vs. STL), but is considered a reliable ratios guy who can score a much-needed win for fantasy managers, as the Brewers will certainly be favorites in that matchup. Gasser earned his fifth win on Saturday, throwing seven scoreless innings against the Orioles. The San Diego Padres took advantage of their four-game series with the Rockies at Coors Field and a home set with the Marlins, scoring 51 runs, 12 more than any other team. Rake Cronenworth was true to his nickname from several years ago. He led all Major League hitters with 13 hits. The Brewers swiped a league-high 12 bags last week: four each for Jackson Chourio and rookie Cooper Pratt. Tampa’s Chandler Simpson led all runners with five swipes, finally catching Washington’s Nasim Nuñez for the MLB lead with 46. Expect Simpson to finish with 50+ and win the stolen base crown.

Of the 29 two-start pitchers excluding Pirates opener Lake Bachar, three earned two wins: Tarik Skubal, Sean Burke and David Peterson. Houston’s Hunter Brown had an outstanding two-step (10 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 5 K – 20 K) and those 20 punchouts led all pitchers for the week. Gavin Williams punched out 16 in 12 innings and is back atop the AL lead in strikeouts with 244. Tampa’s Bryan Baker was the first reliever to reach 40 saves this season. It’s possible that Cade Smith (39), Riley O’Brien (38) and Mason Miller (37) join Baker. It’s possible that attraction towards Ryan Johnson this weekend relates to dynasty and keeper formats, and not his start in Seattle this week. Johnson has limited run damage over his last nine starts, since August 6, posting a 2.39 ERA, but with an xFIP (5.01) nearly double the mark. Johnson is more of a 4.25-4.50 ERA guy than a sub-3.00 ERA one, as his 90.9% LOB and .229 BABIP portends.
Perhaps a similar mindset applies to folks who scooped up Jack Perkins, who pitched two quality starts on the road against the Rays (6.2 IP – 4 H – 0 ER – 1 BB – 8 K) and the Guardians (6 IP – 5 H – 1 ER – 0 BB – 4 K), flashing some of his upside and future potential. Perkins has had a difficult season (5.90 ERA, but a 4.16 xFIP, 1.45 WHIP) and will be a tough streamer at home in Sacramento next season, but the strikeouts (25.2%) should always be there.
Andrew Alvarez should have a rotation spot with the Nationals next season. He has been outstanding since the All-Star break, posting a 2.44 ERA (3.30 FIP, 4.02 xFIP) with a 1.10 WHIP and a 22.7% strikeout rate, though he wasn’t able to secure a win in any of those 10 starts. Alvarez won’t be a particularly coveted target in drafts next season, but should have a NFBC ADP somewhere in the 250-325 overall range. He may be a consideration in NL-only keeper leagues with deep benches and five-plus keepers.
Bold Predictions for Week 27
Gavin Williams and Jacob Misiorowski finish the season tied for the MLB lead in strikeouts with 255. Williams punches out 11 and Misiorowski, eight.
JR Ritchie steps up for his two starts and has a Jack Perkins Week 26 type week, helping managers win league titles.
Cade Cavalli twirls a gem in Detroit this week and pulls his 3.02 ERA under 3.00 to end the season. Cavalli will have a top-60 ADP in 2027.
Jo Adell takes advantage of four left-handed starters this week and earns seven RBIs to reach 100, after falling two RBIs short last season.
One of Cristian Javier or Yusei Kikuchi will remind why streaming pitchers in Sutter Health Park, even if part of a two-step, is a mistake.
Miguel Vargas and Colson Montgomery hit three home runs each this week and the White Sox score the most runs in Week 27.
The Houston Astros win the NL West and knock the Texas Rangers out of playoff contention.
I hope you enjoyed my column this season and that you found it helpful, or at least entertaining and informative. Stay tuned for more from me next week as we hit the offseason streets. Best of luck this final week!
Vlad writes for RotoGraphs and is the head of fantasy baseball content at FTN Fantasy. He is a Tout Wars Expert League champ, member of the CDM Fantasy Sports Hall of Fame and has been nominated for FSWA writing awards six times. Vlad has been playing fantasy baseball since 1995, winning 42 NFBC leagues since 2012 and ranking in the top percentile in NFBC’s Online Championship contest (33% win rate, 52% cash rate; 64 leagues). title: Are the Dodgers finding the best version of themselves just in time?
author: Doug Padilla
body:
LOS ANGELES — The energy emanating from the steamroller heading up I-5 on Monday radiated for miles.
Fuel was used to power the buses the San Diego Padres used to make the trip north for a three-game series that starts Tuesday night, but only because they didn’t try adrenaline.
Winners in 13 of their past 14 games, the Padres are poised to accomplish team history over the next few days. Never in their existence have they made the playoffs in three consecutive seasons.
San Diego has a magic number of two to clinch a National League wild-card spot, although the Padres intend to run through the finish line with a chance at ascending to the top of the wild-card heap in the NL.
“I feel like the whole team is in a good spot right now,” San Diego’s Fernando Tatis Jr. told the San Diego Union-Tribune on Sunday. “We’re playing really good baseball. We’re checking in when we have to. The entire lineup is in a good spot right now. So when it’s going like that, it’s … a good time.”
The Dodgers already have another NL West title secured (their 13th in the past 14 years), but they also have a magic number of three to clinch a top-two seed in the NL playoffs and a bye into one of the best-of-five Division Series.
“I think it’s going to be a good kind of (playoff) primer,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of the upcoming series. “They’re a very talented team. They’re playing as good as anyone in all of baseball. I’m looking forward to playing those guys and just kind of ramping it up a little bit more for our guys.”
With the Dodgers on a 14-3 run since Sept. 3, they are on a familiar final month charge toward the playoffs. Second-half lulls in each of the past two seasons have transformed into Septembers when the group has discovered the best version of itself.
Last season, the Dodgers were swept in a three-game series by the Angels in August then opened September with a three-game dud in Pittsburgh. A disastrous loss in Baltimore lit the fire after Yoshinobu Yamamoto lost a no-hitter with two outs in the ninth inning and the Dodgers never recorded another out while losing the game.
The wide-awake Dodgers went 15-5 the rest of the way, stormed through the NL playoffs – going 9-1 against the Cincinnati Reds, Philadelphia Phillies and Milwaukee Brewers – then came out on top in a dramatic seven-game World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays.
Earlier this month, it was a brutal 8-6 loss in 10 innings to the St. Louis Cardinals on Sept. 2 that was the wake-up call. It included a four-strikeout night from Shohei Ohtani, who played just one more game before taking his current spot on the injured list.
Properly motivated, the Dodgers have gone on a tear ever since, but it has come at the expense of teams that were not in playoff contention like the Washington Nationals, Reds, Miami Marlins and San Francisco Giants.
This week marks the Dodgers’ first chance to face a team playing at the peak of its powers since they faced the Boston Red Sox, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers and Atlanta Braves all in a recent 25-game stretch. They flubbed that test by going 1-12 in those games.
Mookie Betts, Kyle Tucker and Will Smith all have put a charge into the resurgence, while the arrival of rookie Josue De Paula has given the lineup another hitter who can extend at-bats with a discerning eye, along with Max Muncy.
Betts went 0 for 4 in Sunday’s 3-1 victory over the Giants, yet he still is hitting .373 with six home runs, 20 RBIs and a 1.215 OPS in 17 games since the start of September.
Far from content with an offense that has averaged 5.8 runs per game this month, Betts said the Dodgers can do even more. After all, Andy Pages is set to return Tuesday, while Ohtani could be back later this week.
“Some guys are hitting, some guys are not,” Betts said. “I think that’s the beauty of the lineup. You get a couple guys going, and a couple guys here can carry a team, and you never know. You just never know who’s it going to be, it’s different guys every day.”
Amid a brutal first season with the Dodgers, Tucker has done his part lately by going 15 for 36 (.417) over his past 11 games with five home runs and 11 RBIs. He was limited to coming off the bench on Sunday after he fouled a ball off his right knee on Saturday.
Tucker was not with the club for last year’s September revival, but he has helped power this one. When it comes to team potential, Tucker is a big-picture guy.
“I think our potential is winning the World Series,” Tucker said. “So (when) we do that, then I can say we reached it. But we feel like we’re in a good spot right now. Our pitching staff’s done a great job all year giving us an opportunity to win every single night. Our defense has played pretty well behind them and then offensively we’ve done a solid job as well.”
“Right now, we got a few guys that are feeling good. A few guys that are banged up. But we’re still out there grinding trying to win as many games as possible before the season ends and just trying to carry it all the way to the playoffs.”
At the very least, confidence will be high this week, in both dugouts.
UP NEXT
Padres (RHP Michael King, 12-9, 3.03 ERA) at Dodgers (TBA), Tuesday, 7:10 p.m., SportsNet LA, 570 AM

title: What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
author: Lochlahn March
body:
What to watch for as the playoffs loom: Phillies counting on Alex McFarlane, starters as relievers, and more
With their magic number down to three, a fifth straight postseason is in sight for the Phillies. But there are plenty of questions going into the final homestand of the regular season.
The Phillies returned from their final road trip of the season with work to do.
Their magic number to clinch a postseason berth is three. Any combination of wins and Diamondbacks losses that totals three will ensure the Phillies’ season continues beyond Sunday. But while they remain in control of their own destiny, it won’t be easy.
To close out the final week, the Phillies host the top team in the National League in the Brewers, followed by the top team in the American League in the Rays.
Here are a few takeaways heading into the last homestand of the regular season:
Multi-inning McFarlane
The circle of trust in the Phillies bullpen right now is extremely small. The relief unit has a 5.50 ERA in September, and the club took the drastic measure of optioning Orion Kerkering to triple-A Lehigh Valley on Sunday after his struggles became untenable. Unless there is an injury to another member of the staff, he is ineligible to be on the wild-card roster.
While the Phillies’ rotation and closer Jhoan Duran are among the best in the sport, it’s the bridge between them that has been the biggest issue. The Phillies continue to hope Jonathan Bowlan (groin) will be available for the postseason. The right-hander began playing catch Sunday, and reported to the field on Monday’s off day to continue his progress.
Before the injury, Bowlan had been going through a rough stretch, having allowed a run in five of his last six appearances. Even if he were a full go, it would be hard to imagine tossing him right back into an eighth-inning, high-leverage role after spending some time on the shelf.
» READ MORE: Phillies send struggling reliever Orion Kerkering to triple A
Enter Alex McFarlane.
The 25-year-old rookie came through in a big spot against the Mets on Sunday, facing two tough opponents in Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto to get out of a seventh-inning jam. By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.
“I think it is [realistic] this time of year,” Mattingly said. “I mean, I think with Jho, you also get to the point where he’s capable of two innings. You’re just trying to get the guys that we need in the game, for as much as you can.”
So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.
The club is “very optimistic” about Luzardo’s progress from the shoulder inflammation that landed him on the injured list, according to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. Like Bowlan, he has also progressed to playing catch.
Should Luzardo remain on track to return in time for the postseason, Dombrowski said the Phillies are keeping their options open with how they deploy him. It could be as a starter, which might be a risk given his last outing will have been Sept. 7. It could also be as a reliever, a role Luzardo has less experience in, but experience nonetheless. In the deciding Game 4 of the 2025 National League Division Series, he held off the Dodgers for 1⅔ innings of emergency relief in extras, pitching on short rest.
» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

By retiring both of them, McFarlane added a few more notches to his belt, which already included such stars as Shohei Ohtani, Mike Trout, and Nolan Arenado.
But Sunday’s win over the Mets also revealed how interim manager Don Mattingly is planning to handle his relievers in the postseason. After McFarlane struck out Soto to preserve a two-run lead with his 18th pitch, there was initially no movement in the Phillies’ bullpen during the eighth. When the Phillies loaded the bases, that’s when Chase Shugart started getting ready.
Had the Phillies’ lead stayed at two, though, Mattingly was going to send McFarlane back out. Duran would have then started warming to relieve him, and then finish it off in the ninth.
It didn’t wind up happening, but Mattingly envisions using McFarlane and Duran to cover the last nine outs of a close game.

So while the lack of relief depth is still a concern, things will operate a bit differently in the playoffs. The trusted high-leverage arms, as few as they are, can and will be called upon to do more.
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly thinks Chase Shugart can take on a bigger role in Phillies' bullpen
McFarlane has thrown more than one inning just once in the two months he’s been in the majors, covering 1⅓ innings Aug. 15 against the Twins. He said he is ready to do whatever he’s asked.
“Just grateful for the opportunity,” McFarlane said. “Whatever opportunity he gives me, I’m just gonna take it one game at a time. Make sure I prepare my best, and just give all I can anytime he sends me out there.”
Starters in relief
The Phillies still haven’t mapped out how they will deploy their rotation in a wild-card series. That’s because there are a lot of unknowns: whether they will make it at all, who they will play if they do, and the health of Jesús Luzardo.

» READ MORE: The Zack Wheeler conversation: Why he ‘expected’ to thrive after surgery, and how much longer he wants to play
His performance in that role was largely overshadowed by how the game ended, with Kerkering botching a bases-loaded grounder to allow Los Angeles to walk it off. Had Kerkering made the throw to end the inning and things turned out differently, Luzardo’s clutch bullpen appearance might have gone down as legendary instead.
Whether or not Luzardo is one of them, the Phillies bullpen will be getting reinforcements by way of the rotation for the postseason. The question is who.
“Some of our starters are going to end up in the bullpen,” Dombrowski said. “I don’t know how it’s going to work at this point, but some of them will, especially when you get to the first round. We’re going to be the best-of-three, so you only can start three guys at that point. So you got two other guys that can go into the bullpen.”
It’s difficult to see a world where Zack Wheeler or Cristopher Sánchez aren’t starting two of the wild-card games. Aaron Nola has continued his second-half resurgence with a 2.15 ERA since Aug. 3, but he has never been a reliever in any capacity during his major league career, regular season or postseason.
Rookie Andrew Painter continues to be under consideration for making the move. He gave up four runs in his last start against the Mets, but the quality of his stuff remained high. Painter’s first inning especially stood out, when he got Lindor to ground out before striking out Soto and Bo Bichette.
Painter touched 99.4 mph with his fastball in the fifth inning. In a shorter stint, it isn’t hard to imagine him getting into the triple digits.
“I think his stuff will be very solid out there,” Dombrowski said.
» READ MORE: Andrew Painter’s potential role on a Phillies playoff staff is uncertain. Painter says any role is OK with him.
If the opportunity arises in the final six games, Mattingly said he could see the Phillies test-driving that theory by trying Painter out in the bullpen ahead of the playoffs. That said, time is running out.
Painter doesn’t think he necessarily needs a trial run to feel comfortable pitching in relief, however. He has experience with his routine shifting already, pitching behind an opener earlier this year and also appearing in relief after being scratched from his start because of a migraine.
“I feel like postseason baseball, in that atmosphere, the adrenaline is going to be flowing,” Painter said. “I don’t really think there’s much of an adjustment that’s going to be there. I think the adrenaline would just take over from that point.”
More patience from Turner
Whether the Phillies’ offense will get hot at the right time or slide back into a familiar October slumber remains to be seen. But there were some positive signs, particularly from the top of their order, in the series against the Mets.
En route to the series split, it was the top half of the order that carried a lot of the load — excluding a key bases-loaded triple from nine-hole hitter Justin Crawford on Sunday. And that’s how it will need to be for the Phillies to make a deep run.
They didn’t do it with the long ball, as the Phillies’ only two home runs in the series came from Derek Hill and Edmundo Sosa. Instead, they got on base, moved runners, and strung together hits.
Trea Turner in particular had a strong series. He finished 4-for-13 (.308), but the real eye-popping stat was his .526 on-base percentage.
» READ MORE: Can Trea Turner rescue his season despite career-worst stats at the plate? His manager and teammates believe so.
If he could maintain some of that momentum, it would be transformative for the Phillies. What has been a disappointing season by most measures for Turner could be rescued with a strong postseason performance.
“I think more and more, you see how they’re pitching him, and it’s I think basically not throwing him strikes,” Mattingly said of Turner.
According to StatCast, 53.6% of the pitches Turner has seen this year are out of the strike zone. It’s a few percentage points higher than the 51.3% out-of-zone pitches he saw last year, and trails only Kyle Schwarber (54.8%) and Bryce Harper (57.4%) among Turner’s teammates.
The difference has been that Turner swings at those out-of-zone pitches at a much higher clip. His chase rate this year is 34.6%, the second-highest of his career.
But against the Mets, he showed a glimpse of what he could be if he homes in on his selectivity. Turner drew six walks in the four-game series. He also scored three runs.
“The more he walks, the more they’re forced in the strike zone,” Mattingly said. “And when he’s on base, obviously it creates a danger there with him running and things like that. We need him to get on base. When he’s on base, we’re better.”

title: Blue Jays’ Cease won’t need surgery after MRI but season remains in limbo
author: Shi Davidi
body:
BALTIMORE – Somewhat fittingly for a team forced to make TBA a regular part of its starting rotation, Toronto Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease is finishing a Cy-Young calibre season in limbo after an MRI revealed inflammation but no structural damage to his right shoulder.
The 30-year-old, who’s struck out 239 in 169 innings while carrying a 2.40 ERA over 29 starts, said upon rejoining the team Monday that he and the club “are still drafting a plan” for his next steps, although he hasn’t been ruled out from starting again this year.
For him to pitch this weekend against the Cincinnati Reds, manager John Schneider said, Cease will need to be “feeling better with this time down and feeling like himself, and obviously the game meaning a lot” for the Blue Jays, who are nearing elimination in the wild-card race. If not, the first season of his $210-million, seven-year deal will have ended with a messy outing Friday in Texas where his career-low average fastball velocity of 93.6 m.p.h. was concerning enough for him to be sent out for imaging the day after.
“It’s good news, I'm not having surgery, there's nothing that's going to keep me out next year or anything like that,” said Cease. “It's just some inflammation of various kinds.”
Regardless, the disappointing way his season is ending is yet another blow for a Blue Jays rotation that lost Bowden Francis and Shane Bieber before spring training began, Trey Yesavage and Jose Berrios during camp, Cody Ponce 2.1 innings into his first start and Max Scherzer in late April, triggering an ongoing roster churn that had them opening the final week of the season with just two healthy starters.
Even after Yesavage’s activation from his second injured-list stint Monday to start against the Baltimore Orioles, the Blue Jays still had seven starters on the sidelines. A revolving door of arms made “trying to stay mentally positive about it” a challenge, said Schneider, while regular bullpen games meant extra strain on reliever workload not only on the day of, but the days before and the day after, too. There was so much up-and-down that three pitchers, Chad Dallas, also recalled Monday, Chase Lee and Lazaro Estrada, each were optioned the maximum five times allowed without needing to clear waivers.
All of that’s made sustained winning — a 15-14 May and a 17-11 August are their only winning months so far — especially difficult.
“I always say in order to win a few series in a row or to reel off seven or eight in a row, you've got to have a couple turns through the rotation that are pretty good,” said Schneider. “That's been hard to do this year.”
Throughout the season, Cease, along with Kevin Gausman until he was traded, held a threadbare staff together with elite innings every five days, helping to keep a struggling team afloat. But his velocity has been declining for a couple months and he first remembers his shoulder feeling “achy” before his July 25 one-hit, 120-pitch shutout at Boston.
Cease’s fastball averaged 95.8 m.p.h. that afternoon, his first time this season under 96, and hovered in that range through Sept. 2 before dropping to 94.9, 94.8, 93.6 in the three starts that followed.
“I've never really experienced this, it's always been pretty easy for me to throw hard effortlessly. I never really experienced max-effort throwing and it not coming out and all that,” said Cease. “But at the same time it still felt good to compete. And I feel like I've grown a lot as a pitcher in terms of using my pitch mix and executing and locating the fastball and stuff like that. It wasn't anything that was like end of the world. It was just kind of something that had to be dealt with and a part of trying to win is going out and taking the ball, no matter what.”
Trying to describe the feeling in his shoulder, Cease said, “I don't know if I would fully use the word painful, definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal,” and doesn’t believe it resulted from a single moment, but rather the wear and tear “of being a thrower.”
“I will say I think I learned a lot from this year in terms of going forward, how I maybe want to manage things a little better,” he said. “I've learned my body better from a season like this.”
Among the lessons he’s identified is the amount of throwing in-between bullpens he does and finding more opportunities to sneak in additional rest.
Bigger picture, the Blue Jays aim to search for some learnings as to why they’ve had so many pitching injuries this season. Other than playing in the World Series last year, there are no real through lines but they’ve already started looking.
“I think you look at each individual guy and what their workload was this year and what you can try to stay ahead of,” said Schneider. “I feel like we've done a fairly good job with that, with our relievers going back to spring training, trying to ease them in a little bit. And we'll have to look at that again with the number of appearances with some of these guys. We've already started to look at it and start thinking about throwing load in the off-season when it starts, how much rest is going to be needed before you do start and making sure that everyone comes in where they should be next year.”

We've already started to look at it and start thinking about throwing load in the off-season when it starts, how much rest is going to be needed before you do start and making sure that everyone comes in where they should be next year.”

title: Sizzling Padres can punch playoff ticket as soon as opener with Dodgers
body:
Field Level Media
                
22 Sep 2026, 03:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Denis Poroy)
The hottest team in baseball is racing toward a playoff berth, and the San Diego Padres can complete the chase as early as Tuesday's opener of a three-game road series against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
The Padres (87-69) have won 13 of their last 14 games to not only climb out of wild-card uncertainty but also give themselves a legitimate chance at clinching the National League's top wild-card spot over their final six regular-season games.
They can clinch a playoff spot Tuesday with a win and an Arizona Diamondbacks loss to the Colorado Rockies.
A postseason appearance would be the third consecutive for San Diego, which has never delivered a similar run in franchise history.
'This is so fun,' said Jake Cronenworth, who had two home runs and five RBIs for San Diego in its 7-3 home victory over the Miami Marlins on Sunday. 'It's hard to compare each (of the past three playoff chases). Each one's so fun in its own way and unique. But this one's been really awesome.'
Fernando Tatis Jr. added a home run, his 25th, and is batting .310 with 12 home runs and a 1.016 OPS over his past 30 games since Aug. 18.
Against their Southern California rival, the Padres are expected to send right-hander Michael King (12-9, 3.03 ERA) to the mound.
King is 4-0 with a 1.41 ERA over his last five starts and is 1-1 with a 3.12 ERA in three starts against the Dodgers this season, including an outing in May when he went seven scoreless innings. That start included a season-high nine strikeouts.
The Dodgers (96-60) also have plenty to play for after clinching the National League West title last week. They are two games behind the Milwaukee Brewers for the best record in the NL but do not hold the tiebreaker between the teams.
Los Angeles is 14-3 since Sept. 3 and has a magic number of three to clinch a top-two spot in the NL and a bye into the NL Division Series.While the Padres are on a five-game winning streak, the Dodgers have won four in a row after completing a three-game home sweep of the San Francisco Giants.
Tommy Edman hit a game-tying home run in the sixth inning for Los Angeles on Sunday, while Enrique Hernandez had a go-ahead RBI double in the seventh.
While right-hander Roki Sasaki (5-5, 4.60) is set to return from a blister issue, he will have an abbreviated outing and not necessarily as the starter. Manager Dave Roberts characterized the pitching plan as more of a bullpen game.
The Dodgers are also expected to see the return of center fielder Andy Pages for the series opener against the Padres. Pages has not played since Aug. 21 because of a broken hand.
While the Dodgers have found some success over the past three-plus weeks following a lackluster two months, their 14-3 run has not come against teams who are in playoff contention. A visit from the Padres changes that.
'I think it's going to be a good kind of primer,' Roberts said. 'They're a very talented team. They're playing as good as anyone in all of baseball. I'm looking forward to playing those guys and just kind of ramping it up a little bit more for our guys.'
--Field Level Media

title: Guardians can make it simple for clinching a 2026 postseason berth: Keep winning
author: Justin Lada
body:
Baseball season’s marathon is coming down to its final sprint this week, and the Guardians are going to find out if they have enough figurative speed to finish on the podium.
The Guardians did the hard work over the weekend by sweeping the Oakland/Sacramento/not-yet Las Vegas Athletics — though they had to come back on Sept. 18 and 19 — and squeaking out a 1-0 win. But style points don’t matter. Plus-one in the win column is all that counts.
The Detroit Tigers begrudgingly gave Cleveland the slightest bit of help by overcoming a six-run first inning to beat the Chicago White Sox on Sept. 18, 11-8. Unfortunately, their offense didn’t make much noise after that comeback, but it gave the Guardians just enough to climb back atop the AL Central alone.
Now, Cleveland takes its one-game lead in the AL Central and a five-game winning streak to Boston to face the freshly playoff-clinched Red Sox for three games. A series at Boston vs. the Red Sox is almost inarguably the toughest series left for Cleveland, the White Sox, and the rest of the wild card orbit of Texas, Toronto and Houston.
The White Sox will head to Kansas City this week, where the Royals are above .500 at home. Then they come back home to host the Colorado Rockies to end the regular season.
Unfortunately for the Guardians, they don’t have the safety net of any tiebreakers against teams in their orbit. A sweep of the Red Sox would give them the tiebreaker over Boston, but that wouldn’t matter as it would keep them in first place in the division going into the final weekend anyway.
The Red Sox also have their rotation lined up for the wild card Series, likely with the Yankees, since they’re close to having that locked in. Meaning Cleveland gets to face Boston’s best starting arms in Peyton Tolle, ace Sonny Gray, and another lefty in Ranger Suarez. So they all have six days of rest lined up into their starts in three-game wild card series.
Boston is six games back in the loss column of the New York Yankees, so catching them is highly improbable. Will that mean the Red Sox will get some players to rest? Possibly. They might be unlikely to push their starters too hard. But then that’s up to the Guardians’ offense to put them in that position to decide.
By virtue of holding Williams back to pitch last week in the opener vs. the White Sox, he’s not scheduled to pitch again until at least September 25 or 26. Cleveland has Parker Messick going vs. Boston in the opener, which also lines him up for regular rest on the final day of the season on Sept. 27, should Cleveland still need to win that game to get in the postseason.
The division title would be the most advantageous path for Cleveland. It would get a bye to the ALDS and host it at home, though the Guardians just did get their at-home record one game above .500 thanks to a 5-1 home stand to wrap up the regular season at Progressive Field. There is also a scenario in which Texas catches fire this week and clinches the second seed as the AL West champ and relegates Cleveland to a wild-card series no matter what. But for the Guardians, everything right now is about being one game better.
If they manage to win the division, then they can line the rotation up how they want for the ALDS.
If they are still fighting for a wild-card spot heading into the weekend in Kansas City, they would need to decide how they need to use Williams and Messick. If WIlliams starts on September 25, he could go in Game 2 of the wild card series on Sept. 30. If Messick has to pitch for the wild-card spot on Sept. 27, that takes him out of the wild-card round rotation at least on regular rest. At the very least, Cleveland needs the wild card spot wrapped up by Sept. 26, so it can skip Messick on Sept. 27, push him to Sept. 29 and have Messick and Williams lined up for Games 1 and 2.
The Guardians will either finish with another AL Central title, the franchise’s third in a row and the 14th in the history of the division, dating to its first in 1995, the last wild card spot, sending them to the worst division winner, possibly Houston or Texas, and then onto the White Sox IF they get past the wild card round. That means this final road trip could be a four-city, two-week tour to play the most meaningful and stressful baseball all year.
Or: They could miss the playoffs entirely. Thinking about some of those losses earlier in the year at St. Louis and Juan Brito’s error and one of the few Cade Smith blown saves. Or another one of his blown saves during the sweep by the Mets with two outs at home after the trade deadline.
Without having any tiebreakers over teams competing for playoff spots with them, the Guardians have to be one game better than any of them for a playoff spot. Be it the division or the wild card. That means winning one game at a time and just needing to be one run and one game better.

author: MLB com
body:
Pete Alonso lifts a solo home run to right field to cut the Orioles' 3-1 deficit in the bottom of the 1st inning

Six earned in five and two-thirds.
And Pete slams this ball the other way.
It's up, and it's gone.
And Pete Alonso has 39 home runs in his first season as an Oriole, one shy of reaching that round number of 40 once more.
And another home run, KB, to the opposite field.
He leads all of Major League Baseball in home runs to the opposite field.

title: Astros missing playoffs for second straight year may finally force Jim Crane to pivot
author: Scott Barzilla
body:
It might seem like I am an eternal pessimist, but I do believe there are silver linings in every cloud. The Houston Astros got swept by the Atlanta Braves and now trail the Texas Rangers by a game for the AL West crown, and the Chicago White Sox by two games for the last wild card spot. They are going to two cities they do not play well in. In terms of the playoff chase, it does not look good for the hometown nine.
However, behind every challenge is an opportunity. Make no mistake, I am not predicting victory at all. I don't see this road trip going well for a number of reasons. I think a 2-4 finish is likely in the offing and that should not be enough to win the AL West or advance to the wild card. I would be personally ashamed to finish 79-83 and advance to the postseason. However, failing to make the postseason two years in a row and dropping below .500 opens up an opportunity for Jim Crane and company.
They have already jettisoned Dana Brown. They will also jettison Joe Espada if all reporting is true. It is fundamentally impossible to justify keeping him after fading horribly down the stretch. So, how is this an opportunity? Simply put, this team has been hanging on for years. Dusty Baker was a caretaker that just happened to last four seasons. Dana Brown wasn't a serious hire meant to change the direction of the franchise. They just hoped to limp along and see the good times roll.
Espada himself was essentially seen as an extension of Baker. He was a guy that the players seemed to like and they thought that hanging out with Baker since 2020 would rub off on him and keep the magic going. It worked through 2024. Failing this season and failing in the way that they have forces change. Real change. You have a new guy coming in on top and he will hire people under him to usher him.
Change is never easy and often scary, but it brings with it opportunity for the Astros to get things right in the front office and the dugout to stop the downward slide.
It won't be easy. Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, and Christian Walker are all in their mid thirties and highly paid. They aren't likely to get better and more than likely will be a year worse and not a year better. They are roughly making a combined 70 million dollars as well. That is nearly a third of your payroll. A new GM will have to make some dramatic moves because this team is beyond minor tweaks. A new regime gives new opportunities to do that.
It also presents an opportunity to really beat the bushes to hire a new manager. The inside track shouldn't be a part of this equation. They can interview experienced former managers and the younger former players that seem to be the new wave of managers. Again, this is an opportunity for some creativity and a thoughtful process that can produce the best guy for this roster and the roster we will likely have in the next few seasons.
I want my team to win and will always root for them to win, but a part of me is frightened by that outcome. I am frightened by the prospect of winning a horrible division and having that convince Crane and company that they are on the right track. This team has been getting steadily worse since they won the World Series in 2022. Some of that is the natural aging process. Some of that are key players from that team that have moved on. However, most of it is a regime that has kicked the can down the road and spun its wheels because of a lack of vision and a lack of autonomy.
New voices in the front office can solve both of those issues if they are allowed to. Jim Crane has long talked about the importance of winning. He consistently has spent more money than any other owner in Astros history since they have been on the run. He commits plenty of financial resources. It is time to stop the brain drain and bring back smart baseball. The opportunity is there for the taking and now there is no excuse not to get it done.

Dana Brown wasn't a serious hire meant to change the direction of the franchise. They just hoped to limp along and see the good times roll.
Espada himself was essentially seen as an extension of Baker. He was a guy that the players seemed to like and they thought that hanging out with Baker since 2020 would rub off on him and keep the magic going. It worked through 2024. Failing this season and failing in the way that they have forces change. Real change. You have a new guy coming in on top and he will hire people under him to usher him.
Change is never easy and often scary, but it brings with it opportunity for the Astros to get things right in the front office and the dugout to stop the downward slide.
It won't be easy. Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, and Christian Walker are all in their mid thirties and highly paid. They aren't likely to get better and more than likely will be a year worse and not a year better. They are roughly making a combined 70 million dollars as well. That is nearly a third of your payroll. A new GM will have to make some dramatic moves because this team is beyond minor tweaks. A new regime gives new opportunities to do that.
It also presents an opportunity to really beat the bushes to hire a new manager. The inside track shouldn't be a part of this equation. They can interview experienced former managers and the younger former players that seem to be the new wave of managers. Again, this is an opportunity for some creativity and a thoughtful process that can produce the best guy for this roster and the roster we will likely have in the next few seasons.
I want my team to win and will always root for them to win, but a part of me is frightened by that outcome. I am frightened by the prospect of winning a horrible division and having that convince Crane and company that they are on the right track. This team has been getting steadily worse since they won the World Series in 2022. Some of that is the natural aging process. Some of that are key players from that team that have moved on. However, most of it is a regime that has kicked the can down the road and spun its wheels because of a lack of vision and a lack of autonomy.
New voices in the front office can solve both of those issues if they are allowed to. Jim Crane has long talked about the importance of winning. He consistently has spent more money than any other owner in Astros history since they have been on the run. He commits plenty of financial resources. It is time to stop the brain drain and bring back smart baseball. The opportunity is there for the taking and now there is no excuse not to get it done.

title: Yordan Alvarez, Astros enter critical final stretch against Mariners
body:
Yordan Alvarez normally lets his bat do the talking.
But after the Houston Astros were swept in a three-game home series over the weekend by National League East champion Atlanta, Alvarez felt compelled to speak up at a players’ meeting.
“Basically for us, it was three slaps in the face they gave us right in front of our fans, especially,” Alvarez said through an interpreter. “Just use (Monday’s off day) to take it as a reset day and rest, and then the only thing left is to go out there and win the six games we have left.”
The Astros (77-79), who have lost 10 of their past 14 games, enter a two-game series Tuesday at Seattle one game behind Texas in the American League West race. They’ll complete the regular season with four games against the Athletics in West Sacramento, Calif.
Alvarez has held up his end of the bargain. The MVP front-runner leads the AL with a .313 batting average and ranks second in home runs (40) and RBIs (99) as he chases a Triple Crown.
Teammate Taylor Trammell said Alvarez’s words carried weight.
“He doesn’t talk much and when he speaks, there’s a presence,” Trammell said. “This was not a ‘hoorah’ or anything like that. It’s just like, ‘Hey guys, Easy. Just be easy with it,’ and hearing it from him, it means something. You see the way he’s played all year and you can’t tell me there hasn’t been any nicks or bangs for him. And he’s going out there every single day and being the best hitter in the game right now. That’s what he’s doing. And so when he says something and he talks, you listen.”
The Astros, who missed the playoffs on a tiebreaker last season to end an eight-year stretch of postseason appearances, hold the tiebreaker over Texas after winning the season series. The Rangers have three home games against the New York Mets and three games at Minnesota remaining.
The defending AL West champion Mariners (73-83) are five games behind Texas and dropped the season series to the Rangers, leaving them essentially one game from elimination.
They staved that off Sunday as rookie Kade Anderson pitched seven scoreless innings of three-hit ball, with no walks and seven strikeouts, in a 2-1 victory at Colorado.
“You just show up and … keep going,” Mariners catcher Cal Raleigh said. “That’s really all you can do. It’s frustrating, but we made our bed, and we’ve got to lay in it. And it’s our job to show up, play hard and put our best foot forward. It’s baseball, so you never know. Just keep fighting, keep battling, try to win one pitch at a time, and you know the rest is what it is.”
Tuesday’s series opener is set to feature a pair of right-handers, the Astros’ Cristian Javier (2-6, 5.31 ERA) and the Mariners’ Logan Gilbert (12-10, 3.69).
Javier suffered a 5-2 loss to visiting Kansas City last Wednesday, despite allowing just two runs over 5 1/3 innings. He’s 3-2 with a 2.87 ERA in nine career appearances against Seattle, including six starts.
Gilbert is coming off a 2-1 loss last Tuesday to the Angels in Anaheim, Calif., despite a quality start of six innings with two runs allowed. He’s 7-4 with a 3.18 ERA in 15 career starts against the Astros. Gilbert was the winning pitcher in a 6-1 victory April 12 in Seattle as he allowed one run on four hits over seven innings, with one walk and seven strikeouts.
–Field Level Media
